items.title: In photos: The enduring resistance of Notting Hill Carnival
items.excerpt: Carnival of Resistance — A new photobook by Wayne Campbell and Wayne Crichlow reflects on the protest beginnings of Europe’s biggest street festival, along with the traditions keeping its original spirit alive today. N
items.content:
Carnival of Resistance — A new photobook by Wayne Campbell and Wayne Crichlow reflects on the protest beginnings of Europe’s biggest street festival, along with the traditions keeping its original spirit alive today.

Notting Hill Carnival always evokes sharp visions in the imagination. Intricate floats. The technicolour, feathered outfits of mas bands. Eardrum bursting reggae, dub, jungle and UK garage of the soundsystems. Jerk chicken, curry goat and rice and peas. Huge, pulsing crowds that file through the area’s streets. Or for its critics, it represents disorder, noise, and unpoliceable chaos.

But lesser remembered is its place as a protest. In 1958, severe and violent race riots broke out in the West London neighbourhood, as mobs of white gangs armed with sticks, bottles, bricks and knives attacked homes and businesses of Black people. In response, a year later in 1959, journalist and activist Claudia Jones – who was born in Trinidad and Tobago and moved to the UK after being imprisoned in the US in the ‘Red Scare’ – organised a party at St Pancras Town Hall.

There were steel pan bands, singers and dancers, as the cultural celebration protested violence and racism with music and dancing. The event was an early blueprint for resistance through joy and celebration of culture, which eventually inspired the first official Notting Hill Carnival in 1966. “There was the murder of [Antiguan migrant] Kelso Cochrane that was dividing communities,” explains photographer Wayne Campbell, co-author of a new photobook Carnival of Resistance, which is published as the festival celebrates 60 years of existence.

  • Read next: Notting Hill Carnival 2023: an oral history of all-female sound systems

“A lot of tension existed within the Afro-Caribbean community that had come over just after Windrush, and it felt like something needed to be done,” he continues. “Ironically, what happened came not with knives and sticks but with heritage and culture. And so was born the Notting Hill Carnival.”

Ever since, the August Bank Holiday celebration of the Afro-Caribbean diaspora, and its diverse cultures in the UK, has bloomed to become Europe’s largest street festival, growing and iterating across the decades. Yet underneath the noise, outfits and party façade, the original protest spirit remains alive through rituals and traditions.

These are the focus of Carnival of Resistance, which is made in conjunction with fellow photographer and Carnival regular Wayne Crichlow. Both photographers have been involved with Notting Hill Carnival since they were young. They’ve been photographing the event for years, with the pair also having performed there in their younger years. Campbell was part of a steel pan band, while Crichlow was in dance music group Closer Than Close.

  • Read next: A look down the side streets at Notting Hill Carnival

“It was the main stage, typical bank holiday weekend – it was raining, and I was playing the synth,” Crichlow remembers. “I played this bassline, and I remember playing my first note and the sound engineer on the other side of the field was freaking out, because they weren’t expecting the levels. The particular track was very bass heavy, but it was just absolutely brilliant.”

Carnival of Resistance collates photographs that the pair have taken over the past 15 years. Yet it shines a different light on the weekend’s proceedings to the usual maximalist, colour-forward images of Carnival, subverting stereotypical imagery through Campbell’s black-and-white photos featuring just a strip of colour, along with Crichlow’s street shots that embrace grit and reality.

“We wanted to remind people that Carnival was all about resistance,” Crichlow continues. “It was about the emancipation from slavery, pushing back against racism, and the community. Carnival is not just about getting drunk, eating your rice and peas and dancing very intimately with strangers – there’s an underlying seriousness.”

  • Read next: On the frontlines of Britain’s ’80s protest movements

There’s a chapter on J’ouvert – the Trinidadian originating tradition where people gather before dawn to ring in the carnival with a huge splash of oil, chocolate, paint and more, with the ritual being derived from slaves who would burn sugarcane fields to resist against their slave masters. Elsewhere, there are photos of Jab Jab, where people cover themselves in black oil and charcoal, while wearing horns and chains as direct symbolic expression of emancipation from slavery. 

One picture pays tribute to Grenfell Tower, which overlooks the celebrations and stands as a reminder of continued inequalities, while another photo shows a girl dancing on her own in the foreground while holding up a plastic bottle, with three Metropolitan Police officers on motorbikes stationary behind her. Despite existing now for 60 years, when Carnival rolls around each August it comes under scrutiny, often with op-ed attacks from the right wing press over its cost to the taxpayer, or complaints by the police about the strain the event puts on its officers. Occasionally, politicians raise the idea of moving the celebration to Hyde Park to make it easier to regulate.

Campbell explains that its critics are missing the bottom line. “For the Notting Hill area and that part of the community, Carnival makes hundreds of millions of pounds,” he says. According to research commissioned by The Voice, Carnival’s net economic impact is close to £400 million each year. “Local businesses and the extended area make so much money in a very short period of time. People come from abroad, and it boosts London’s economy, but there will always be a small percentage of people who are sure that it shouldn’t exist, or use it as a political football to say X or Y.”

  • Read next: Photos capturing the soul of Notting Hill in the ‘70s

Ultimately, as long as Carnival is treated politically by mainstream society, its presence will always be a protest. “In the ’60s, a lot of those houses in West London were squats, so a lot of people in the [Afro-Caribbean] community settled there,” Crichlow says. “So Carnival is not only keeping the original spirit alive, but it’s actually reclaiming our streets. You may want to pile in a load of money, bring in faceless investors and price us out, but even if it’s only three days a year, we’re going to take our streets back.”

items.title: Capturing Time: Review of the Zero Image Pinhole Camera by Taylor Blanchard
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Taylor Blanchard

I have a few cameras that feel like an extension of me: cameras that produce images that most reflect who I am and help me creatively express my ideas. My Zero Image Pinhole is one of those cameras.

It’s not necessarily easy to use, but at its heart, it’s the embodiment of film photography – light passing through a small aperture and recording an image on film. No batteries, no lenses, no image framing window.

Find the Zero Image Pinhole Camera at the Zero Image website.

As the pandemic was ramping up in early 2020, Blue Moon Camera sent an email that they were receiving a shipment of cameras from Zero Image, a Hong Kong-based camera company that makes wooden cameras in a variety of formats.

Zero Image was shutting down for the foreseeable future given stay-at-home restrictions. In the U.S., we were a few weeks away from that fate. I’m not sure what resonated with me most: the beautiful wood camera? The thought of purchasing a camera from a company that couldn’t make cameras for a while? Or a typical case of GAS (gear acquisition syndrome)? 

Whatever the reason, I clicked “add to cart” – buying one of the medium format (120 film) models. A few months later, well into stay-at-home orders in the U.S., the camera arrived. It was as beautiful as I had imagined, and quite intimidating. While it’s a simple rectangle box camera, it doesn’t look or feel easy to shoot in the way a plastic camera or a point and shoot does. 

Zero Image was launched in 1999 by Zernike Au, a “pinhole enthusiast” who had a successful career as a product designer, according to the company’s website. When Zero Image launched, its website says there wasn’t another roll film pinhole camera company in existence. The cameras are constructed of teak wood and brass and finished with a wax or varnish, depending on the model. Several retailers carry the brand, but the cameras are often out of stock.

Unboxing and Setting Up the Zero Image Pinhole Camera

There are several models of Zero Image; I bought the 69D Deluxe “Back to Nature” edition. I think it’s named “Deluxe” because it comes with added features: a bubble level, a 52mm filter thread, and a cable release adapter (the naming of these cameras is a bit confusing to me). All the 69 models can shoot 6×4.5, 6×6, 6×7, and 6×9. Back to nature refers to the wood finish: a wood oil versus a varnish.  

Zero Image pinhole cameras arrive in a subtle cardboard box. The camera comes with a basic instruction manual that provides a basic overview of loading film, exposing film, and caring for the camera.

As I mentioned, the camera design is simple. On the front of the camera is the filter thread, a brass cable release adapter, and the shutter. The pinhole size is 0.17mm and the focal length is 40mm for an equivalent aperture opening of f/235.

The top of the camera has two brass knobs – one to lock the top wood plate in place; the other is a film advance winder. The bubble level is also on top of the camera. The back of the camera has a sliding cover with 3 red windows to reveal the film count: the upper window is for 6×4.5, the middle is for 6×6, and the bottom is for 6×7 and 6×9. There is also a brass dial on the back which acts as an exposure scale to guide your exposure calculations. 

To adjust the film format size and load the film, remove the top cover and then slide out the back cover. Two dividers allow you to adjust the aspect ratio. I generally shoot the same aspect ratio with this camera, although you could adjust it every time you load film.

The film loads on the left side of the camera; the film moves from left to right. Loading the camera can be a bit tricky, even once you’re accustomed to the process. You drop the film into the right side slot and then roll the 120 paper leader onto the take-up spool, ensuring the spool snugly fits behind a metal guide. You then slide the back cover on and fasten the top onto the camera. You must line up the slot on the take up spool with the film advance knob. Finally, tighten the center knob.

Then, turn the film advance knob clockwise to move the film. You move the film until the number 1 appears in the window that matches the format that you set. The red window is similar to several other cameras with red windows, like a Holga or Brownie.

Related: An Overview of Pinhole Film Photography: Exposure, Reciprocity, & 6 Cameras I Love

Moving from ‘Meh’ to ‘Marvelous’

The first year or so I owned this camera, I enjoyed it, but I didn’t connect with the camera. I thought the exposures didn’t render the results that I expected. Following the exposure dial on the back of the camera and using a light meter app, I felt like all my shots were way under- or over-exposed, and I didn’t like the images I was getting. I muddled along with the camera, never loving it.

Then, two things changed. First, I adjusted the aspect ratio from 6×6 to 6×9. I’m not sure why I defaulted to shooting 6×6 when I first got the camera, as I already have several cameras that shoot that format. I find it easier to frame my photos and pre-visualize the scene with 6×9, since it’s almost as wide as the camera. The 6×9 format also creates more expansive images (and, yes, I eventually want a camera that shoots 6×12).

Next, my friend Alec Pain helped me with the exposure calculations. To get more accurate exposures, I follow the multi-step process that he later published for Shoot It With Film. The two biggest changes I made were calculating the exposure specifically for f/235 and then accounting for the reciprocity characteristics of the film. Before I had been winging it with exposure, which can sometimes lead to good results, but never consistent results.

I started to play more with the camera and push the limits of shooting with it. Instead of always reaching for a film with a good reciprocity quality, I would look in my reciprocity app for the films that need multiple minutes of light for a minute of measured exposure. I frequently use filters, typically a red or IR filter, which add even more exposure time, for creating self-portraits or photographing the environment around me. The results of these long exposures feel like capturing time as a continuum and not a fixed instant.

With these changes, the camera is the one I turn to for many ideas and projects. I love carrying it when I travel, even though it takes more effort to use. It’s one way to capture a frequently photographed scene in a new way.

One of My Favorite Cameras, Broken

As I was pondering the outline for this article, the worst happened: the camera started to wobble on the tripod, so I unscrewed the tripod plate to investigate – accidentally pulling off the tripod thread and the wood that was holding it in place. That point of the camera is often under pressure with the tripod, plus I am often taking the tripod plate off to move to another camera, which might add additional tension. I emailed Blue Moon Camera to see if they had any ideas, and someone named Jed (I think) called me back.

He’d had the same thing happen to his Zero Image camera and we chatted through some ideas on how to fix it. I ended up screwing the plate back into the camera, slightly offset from the previous screw holes into wood that is still stable. Next, I need to get a product like Liquid Nails to secure it further.

It’s something to keep in mind with this, or any wood camera. I always keep mine stored in a Domke wrap, in a plastic bin with some silica gel packets. But, I also tote it around with me, and it’s definitely been dinged up and exposed to the elements.

I thought the tripod base would have been sturdier and, honestly, am a bit surprised that the wood would have become that soft. I also found it reassuring that it happened to someone else, although it begs the question how many other people have experienced this issue?

Conclusion

While anyone can make a pinhole camera with household materials (and it’s a fun activity for kids and adults), generally you don’t have as much control. With a Zero Image (or similar brand) pinhole, you know the exact aperture opening and can calculate your exposures. It’s an amazing camera to test the limits of a film stock and push yourself creatively.

The wood is gorgeous and eye-catching and often prompts conversations with passersby. I would hope that subsequent versions of the camera have a stronger base for the filter thread. I’ll continue to use the camera for as long as possible, even if I have to keep gluing it!

What do you think of these wood pinhole cameras? Let me know what you think in the comments!

Thank you so much, Taylor! Taylor is a regular contributor here at Shoot It With Film, and you can check out her other articles here, such as Phoenix vs. Ektachrome: Is Harman’s Color Film a Slide Film Alternative? and Shooting Film on a Budget: Color Films Under $10.

You can also check out more of Taylor’s work on Instagram.

Leave your questions about the Zero Image Pinhole Camera below in the comments, and you can pick one up for yourself on the Zero Image website.

items.title: Polaroid releases new cameras and film to mark 30 years of Pokémon
items.content:
Polaroid has announced its biggest special edition yet to mark the 30th anniversary of the Japanese video game and trading card franchise Pokémon.

Polaroid is releasing no less than three Pokémon-branded Polaroid cameras, along with three special-edition films and three different accessories.

The camera line-up includes two full-sized Now Gen 3 camera, as well as a smaller Go Gen 3 camera.

The different cameras are:

  • Special edition Now Gen 3 – Pokémon design in red, white and black
  • Special edition Go Gen 3 – Pikachu design in yellow and black
  • Special edition Go Gen 3 – Sylveon design in blue, white and pink

The Pokémon camera costs £129.99 in the UK, $139.99 in the US and €139.99 in the EU. The Pikachu and Sylveon cameras cost £89.99 in the UK, $99.99 in the US and €99.99 in the EU.

The three new films are all include Pokémon frames and are as follows:

  • Polaroid Color i-Type Film – Pokémon Edition: (£21.99/$22.99 /€21.99)
  • Polaroid Go Color Film – Pokémon Pikachu Edition – Double Pack: (£21.99/$24.99 €22.99)
  • Polaroid Go Color Film – Pokémon Sylveon Edition – Double Pack: £21.99 / $24.99/€22.99)

The cameras and films are joined by a case, a branded photo album and a special Pokémon strap.

All the new Pokémon-branded products are expected to be available from 25 August.

Polaroid said in a press release: “Celebrating 30 years of Pokémon, the collection marks Polaroid’s biggest collaboration yet and includes three cameras, three film frames with custom dark slides and iconic accessories.

“The products have been designed to bring Pokémon’s playful energy to Polaroid’s iconic cameras, while encouraging both younger and older fans of Pokémon to embrace the tactile, analogue joy of shooting with Polaroid.”

“Pokémon has always been about discovery, connection, and exploration. Working with Polaroid feels like a natural extension of these values: encouraging fans to capture moments that matter most to them in their own way and turn their favourite memories into tangible keepsakes,” said Mathieu Galante, The Pokémon Company International’s senior director of licensing.

items.title: Four Shortlisted Artists Stand to Win the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize 2026
items.content:
Four Shortlisted Artists Stand to Win the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize 2026

August 19, 2026
Photography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

From nearly 4,000 entries submitted by 1,338 photographers around the world, a striking selection has been shortlisted for the Winston Taylor Photo Portrait Prize 2026. The handpicked images represent some of the finest photographic portrait work being made today, from intimate settings in which figures meet the viewer’s eye to candid scenes on city streets and rural expanses alike.

Open to professionals and amateurs alike, the competition will select one winner to receives a £15,000 award plus a commission to be added to the collection of London’s National Portrait Gallery. An exhibition of the best entries will also be shown at the museum from November 5 to January 17, and the winner will be announced on November 3.

The four shortlisted images include Max Pattenden’s tender “Havannah, Lee Moor,” James Clifford Kent’s “Neisser, Pinar del Río, Cuba,” Marcie Docherty’s “PE,” and Katie Hitchcock-Smith’s dusky “Moroccan (Amazigh) Cowboys.” Learn more and plan your visit on the museum’s website.

items.title: Inside Yoshiwara, Japan’s oldest red light district
items.excerpt: Asasuka soaplands — Despite numerous fires and harshening sex work laws, the centuries old area continues to persevere in East Tokyo. Manami Okazaki traces its history and meets people who shape its present. It is earl
items.content:
Asasuka soaplands — Despite numerous fires and harshening sex work laws, the centuries old area continues to persevere in East Tokyo. Manami Okazaki traces its history and meets people who shape its present.

It is early evening in Yoshiwara, a sizeable block of buildings north of Asakusa, East Tokyo, just a stone’s throw from Sensoji temple – one of most visited tourist attractions in Japan. The streets are somewhat quiet, but there are black vans with tinted windows outside most of the buildings and a noticeable amount of carparks. Brothels sit side by side – around 140 of them – lit with ’80s looking signs with glowing neon lettering reading ‘Moulin Rouge’, ‘Etoile’ and ‘Good Wife’. Bouncers dressed in suits stand outside the building, while girls, mostly in their 20s, enter the buildings. 

Despite Yoshiwara being considered to be Japan’s top red-light district, with most high-end joints charging up to ¥80,000 (£370) to ¥100,000 (£460) for 120 minutes, it looks like a town trapped in time. Buildings look like relics from the bubble era, with a kitsch, retro vibe and the entire atmosphere of the district is reminiscent of a film from a lost decade, just before the economy folded. 

Yoshiwara itself has a storied history, which goes back to the Edo era (1600-1868), and was developed by the shogun to restrict the widespread sex trade to a confined area. First established in Ningyocho, it moved to the current Senzoku area after a fire burnt the original location to cinders. Fires have destroyed Yoshiwara numerous times, yet it has been constantly rebuilt, and even survived prostitution’s criminalisation in 1958. 

Due to modern Adult Entertainment Business laws, new brothels in the area can’t easily be established, so many existing buildings are refurbished, rather than replaced. Added to that are strict zoning laws, which make it incredibly difficult to simply open up shop. And though there exists an arguably high societal tolerance for commercial sex entertainment, it may not be around for much longer – it’s questionable whether Yoshiwara will survive these legal restraints in the upcoming decades. 

  • Read next: The intricate, clandestine art of Japan’s traditional tattoos

Edo bordellos

When perusing ukiyo-e – traditional wood block prints dating back to the Edo era, one of Japan’s most exalted art forms – one will invariably find hundreds, if not thousands of depictions of Yoshiwara denizens. Exaggerated female portraits of women donned with a gaudy number of hairpins, scenes from overcrowded brothels and couples in impossibly bendy poses in coitus. While most museums often euphemistically refer to the portraits as “beauties”, many of the women depicted are courtesans, characterised by their make-up and embellishments, and layers of colourful clothing. They were considered celebrities during the time among the commoner class and exalted as fashion and style mavens.

The Edo era was a period of peace, unlike the previous ages which were fraught with civil conflict and war. Wealth accumulated, there was a sense of freedom and consumer power, even among the lower stratum of society. A hedonistic ethos and ‘live for the moment’ attitude dominated urban life for the commoners who were engaged with the pleasure quarters and entertainment districts. The culture of teahouses and kabuki theatre was celebrated in these artworks, which served as a form of media during the time. While what was called the ‘floating world’ is that of everyday decadence, simultaneously there are poetic allusions to the ephemeral and transitory nature of life.

Sumptuary laws tried to restrict the flaunting of ostentatious wealth and hedonistic pursuits of the commoners. When an official decree was put in place to censor courtesan pictures; woodblock artists of the commoner class often had an anti-authoritarian mentality and never stopped, usually skirting around these laws. Many of the famous artists of the time created pieces showing cat protagonists in the likenesses of their favourite courtesans, decked out in layers of fabrics, carrying fans, and sitting around in a brothel.

While depictions of Yoshiwara are glamorous, life for the courtesans of the Edo was anything but. Researchers Stephen and Ethel Longstreet in their book Yoshiwara describe the labour as being akin to slavery and debt bondage. Many girls were sold by their family, while “melancholia made them its victims. Anxiety, hysteria and neuroses were common,” as were disease and alcoholism.

  • Read next: Photos that capture the red lights of ’70s Paris

Yoshiwara today

Yoshiwara nowadays has the same paradox as times of yore. While celebrated in art and culture, and prostitution is somewhat tolerated, even accepted among many people, there is still the official notion that it simply shouldn’t be mentioned, and in some cases, it is treated like it doesn’t, and shouldn’t exist. 

While there have been recent depictions of Yoshiwara in popular culture in Japan, such as the TV show Berabou (Unbound) and exhibitions about the district, including a major show at the Tokyo Fine Arts School University Art Museum, there is no mention of the fact that Yoshiwara still stands. The district is not mentioned on maps and can only be located by looking up ‘Senzoku 4-chome’. 

Nowadays, the area does not have the Edo era moat and girls trapped in tea houses that resemble a large wooden bird cage like the days of yore. Rather, Yoshiwara is dominated by ‘soaplands’, which are a type of brothel where workers massage and perform intimate services for clients in a room with a large bath.

  • Read next: Inside Japan’s most notorious Love Hotel

Sweet Kiss is one such soapland in Yoshiwara, which is on the cheaper end and employs around 70 women. Female manager Kana Ookawauchi says, “We have customers who are in their 20s, but mostly it is people in their 40s and 50s. Some of them are like grandpas. I think people who come to an inexpensive shop like ours for a short time tend to want stimulation, rather than a deep relationship.”

The rooms are small, tiled and somewhat spartan. There is a bath, and a large inflatable bed that looks like a pool toy. The other half of the room has a hard massage bed, and in the corner is a strange vertical box, which is ostensibly a sauna, as by Japanese law, full-service sex work is illegal. Legally, these brothels are in fact saunas and any sex that takes place is due to the worker and the john supposedly having spontaneous, consensual, non-commercial sex during a professional sauna service. 

Ookawauchi says that the women who work there are mostly in their 20s and 30s, although there are many older women as well. She herself was also a former worker and she says that during the time, she wanted to spend money on her idols, travel and get plastic surgery, which is the case with many girls nowadays, in that they are fueled by their interests, rather than being forced by destitution.  

Itsuki is one such girl at Sweet Kiss, who does sex work “to save money and spend on her hobbies”. She doesn’t have many qualms about what she does and has no desire to quit. She explains, “I usually wake up at 10:30am and stay there until 5pm or 6pm. I wait in the waiting room and when a customer comes in, and I’m assigned a room. When I’m done, I clean up. I have a lot of customers, usually four or five people [a day] and on average 80 minutes per booking.” Lately, due to the cheap yen, Japan has become a destination for sex tourism. Itsuki says, “I have more foreign customers from Asia, the most common is Chinese, Taiwanese and Korean as well as westerners and Africans.”

  • Read next: Inside the weird world of audio porn

Beniko’s world

Beniko Iromachi is a photographer who documents Japan’s red-light districts. She was a sex worker for 13 years and retired when she was 32 years old. Rather than disavow her past, Iromachi decided to document these areas in vivid tones, which capture the lustful hues of the neon lights, and the minutiae of the rooms. She first picked up a camera at 48 years old, and she approaches her subject matter with authority and affection. Her personal experiences shape her unique eye and insight into details that reveal the language of codes and symbols underpinning the economy of intimacy.

“I hardly went to school, so I couldn’t read or write very well. After doing this work, I couldn’t really get a job. I was very depressed and I was working at an adult goods store, cleaning the products. I thought I should be ashamed of myself, I didn’t have anything I could say about my past to people, and I just thought that I would end my life like this, living in regret,” Beniko explains. “It’s not seen well socially and you wouldn’t be able to get a job if you were outed. Also, if there’s something political, like sex worker rights related, the sex worker’s opinion should be heard, but I don’t think there’s a lot of people who want to hear the voices from people on the ground.”

Walking around Yoshiwara, we drop by a small bookstore called Kastori that specialises in sex work topics where Beniko is holding an exhibition. Due to media exposure with mainstream magazines and newspapers, Beniko’s larger shows sometimes receive 1,000 visitors over a 10 day period. She also hosts tours on occasion to show the lay of the land. When we reach the entrance of Yoshiwara, where the Edo era gates were once located, she points out a massive curve in the road.

  • Read next: New exhibition spotlights the ongoing impact of Japanese Women Photographers

“The topography of the district is the same as the Edo era. There is a massive bend in the main road in order to protect the privacy of the customers who come into the area.” We also pass by the Yoshiwara Benzaiten shrine, where 490 women were trapped in the blazes of the Great Kanto Earthquake that completely destroyed Yoshiwara – in fact fires destroyed the district at least 20 times. These women tried to save their lives by jumping into the pond that is still there, and is now inhabited by carps.

“Since I started photographing these places, my view of life has changed a lot.” Beniko says, “Rather than feel remorse about my past, I want to document the historic red-light districts all over the country. For me, Yoshiwara is a place that helped me when I had nowhere else to go. Preserving these buildings as they exist now, is also an impetus for my work as Yoshiwara might not even exist in a few decades time. While some people might not want to acknowledge it exists, I view Yoshiwara as a form of culture.” 

Manami Okazaki is a journalist and author based in Tokyo. Follow her on Instagram.

items.title: Film in the Florida Keys by Caitlin Cisar
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Today, we’re featuring a wonderful Florida Keys photo story from film photographer Caitlin Cisar. Scroll below to view the images and read more from Caitlin about exploring the Keys…

Analog cameras and films used: Minolta X-7A (Find on eBay) | Kodak Gold 200 (Find on Amazon), Lomography LomoChrome Turquoise (Find on Amazon)

Connect with Caitlin: Website

Film in the Florida Keys

By Caitlin Cisar

Flying with film means I always play the fun-time-at-airport-security-game where I ask them to handcheck my bag of film. Honestly, it’s a bit of a hassle for everyone so I get it; but this trip I tried something different. I pre-purchased my development and brought a bubble mailer with me so I could drop it in the post-office before catching my flight back home.

I headed to the Florida Keys with a roll of Kodak Gold 200, LomoChrome Turquoise 100-400, and my trusty Minolta X-7A + Minolta 50mm F/2 lens. Part of why I love shooting film is because I love the simplicity and tactile experience of this camera and lens. I zoom with my feet, manually set the exposure with my in-viewfinder meter, and hold my breath when the shutter speed is low.

I also love to try experimental stocks, which is why I included a roll of Turquoise in my bag. I started in Key Largo (the top island of the Keys) and chose ISO 400. I am always pleasantly surprised with color shift film; while I know things will be different, exactly which other worldly effects are a fun surprise. Jurassic Park vibes were not on my radar, but I love the result!

Kodak Gold is my everyday film stock otherwise, and I figured it would be especially nice for some leisurely travel photos in a tropical setting. There’s something already warm about both the color and contrast combination, and it can really work for a range of situations. I loaded this next and headed south.

The Florida Keys have a rich history. A must-do for history buffs is a stop at Pigeon Key, which is accessible by walking, bicycle, or tram across the old Seven Mile Bridge. Renting bikes made the 4-mile trek a breeze (literally) which was a nice reprieve from the heat.

Upon arriving at Pigeon Key, there is a small fee to explore the island. You get access to bathrooms, a gift store, a museum, and if you time it right, you can see the shark feeding.

The story goes that the pool used to be for humans—those who worked on the bridges and railways. Eventually it was taken over, and the new owner removed a corner to accommodate boat parking. Sometime later, with the current ownership, the pool is now home to sharks and fish exclusively. Every month the gates are opened and the sharks can swim out, however, they always return, likely because it is a safe home for them. Edgar (the bird) also lives on the island full-time.

Heading further south to the bottom of the Keys is Key West, which has the famous (and busy) Duval Street filled with restaurants, bars, roosters, and beautiful architecture. A stroll that is worth a few shots on Gold around sunset.

After finishing the film rolls, I dropped the mailer off at a post office and hopped on my flight care-free. A week later, the photos were in my inbox. This was nice not only to avoid traveling back with the film and then deal with packing it up, but it also motivated me to truly “shoot it with film.” Having a deadline and mission made me excited to spend time taking photos as one of my travel activities. I’ll definitely be doing this method again and am excited to try out different stocks in new locations!

items.title: Kosmo Foto’s Direktor walk with the Photographer’s Gallery Bookshop
items.content:
In May, Kosmo Foto originally planned with the help of the Photographer’s Gallery Bookshop to unveil our latest film.

Kosmo Foto Direktor is a limited-edition re-rolled version of Eastman Kodak’s peerless 5222 XX black-and-white cinema film which has been used in iconic films such as ‘Raging Bull’, ‘Casino Royale’ and ‘Oppenheimer’.

Kosmo Foto was released in time for the Photographica camera fair in London in May.

The walk had to be postponed in May, but is now taking place this Saturday (22 August). The Direktor walk will be the only photo walk featuring this film. It will be starting at The Photographers Gallery on Ramilles Street at 11am.

Tickets cost £20 including VAT. Each ticketholder will get a roll of Direktor – which is not available in the shops and can only be ordered from Kosmo Foto.

The walk will work its way through central London visiting various landmarks from cinema history – and we’re challenging you to think like a director, taking shots you think could be stills from a film.

There will also be some spot prizes from Kosmo Foto and its online camera shop Cameraburo.

A note on Direktor: we had originally planned to follow the original version of Kosmo Foto Direktor with further batches in a metal canister, but the cost of producing the film was slightly higher than we’d anticipated. We’d prefer to keep our films as affordable as possible, so unless we can find a cheaper method of producing it, this will be the only batch of the film we will produce.

If you can’t make the walk on Saturday and you still fancy shooting it, head to the Kosmo Foto Shop.

items.title: Fotohane Darkroom
Lost photos from the heyday of punk and new wave
items.excerpt: Crash Bang — DB Burkeman’s latest photobook unearths photographs from his younger years as an aspiring music photographer, which sat undeveloped in his family home for decades. After his mother died, DB Burkeman return
items.content:
Crash Bang — DB Burkeman’s latest photobook unearths photographs from his younger years as an aspiring music photographer, which sat undeveloped in his family home for decades.

After his mother died, DB Burkeman returned to the family’s London home to clean out his childhood bedroom. There, he discovered a clear plastic bag filled with some 30 rolls of undeveloped black and white film – artefacts from his brief but wondrous stint as a rock & roll photographer at the turn of the 1980s. “I had thrown them into this drawer, thinking I’ll get to them later, but I was a bit of a mess,” Burkeman says. “The priority for me was never being a professional photographer. I would tell people that’s what I was doing, but the reality was [something else].”

Growing up in London during the ’70s, Burkeman remembers how stagnant youth culture had become, as he saw arena rock churning out a generation of clones. “Before ’76, everybody looked the same. It was just a sea of denim, right? It was just flared, flared jeans, jean jackets, and long hair,” he says. “Then all of a sudden there was this seismic shift where the Pistols had ripped a hole and changed the perception of what a rock band could be. There were 100 bands in London playing every night, and you only had to pay three quid, instead of £30, to see Eddie and the Hot Rods or the Damned. Everybody cut their hair and got rid of their flares. Everything just changed.”

Inspired, Burkeman dropped out of school at 16. Although he would later become a DJ, bringing jungle to New York in the ’90s, his musical talents lay dormant in his youth. But all was not lost. He explains, “I loved the image of the photographer; it’s almost like being a rock star. You were important, but you were also hiding behind, if not a guitar or drums, a camera.”

  • Read next: Riot grrrl is back. Do we need it more than ever?

But as a teen, business never came before pleasure, or quite frankly at all. “I knew I had a good eye, but I didn't have the people skills to really be able to pull it off,” Burkeman says. But that didn’t stop him from dreaming of becoming the next David Bailey or having a romp like David Hemmings in Blow-Up – only to discover reality is, indeed, the strangest fantasy of all. 

Although half of the film negatives had been lost to the ravages of time, the images that remained form an intoxicating portrait of the era. With the publication of Crash Bang: Pictures from a Punk (Blurring Books), Burkeman returns to where it all began: his years spent in London, New York, and Los Angeles between 1976 and 1982. 

  • Read next: Coming of age in New York’s ’70s punk heyday

As a budding rock photographer, Burkeman was the consummate insider, snapping scenes of musicians in their element. The Ramones rock out at the Rainbow and Alice Bag hangs out at home, while Sid Vicious and Nancy Spungen stride proudly out of Westminster Magistrate’s Court with their heads held high. Like many of his contemporaries, Burkeman developed a taste for heroin that eventually brought an end to his time on the scene. 

Today, the lost photographs fill a void in more ways than one. “I have a notoriously bad memory,” he says. “I did way too much acid between the ages of 14 and 16, and the psychiatrist told me that later in life, it would hurt my memory. I was like whatever, but sure enough he’s right.”

Crash Bang: Pictures from a Punk by DB Burkeman is published by Blurring Books.

items.title: Harlem Labs: Survival and Ambition
items.content:
Harlem has always been more than a neighborhood; it is a living, breathing inheritance. From the electrifying heights of the Harlem Renaissance to the contemporary street corners that dictate global fashion and art, it remains a sanctuary where culture is forged, tested, and passed down. Drawing inspiration from the iconic narrative of The Wiz, a new visual project from Harlem Labs honors that deep legacy while charting an entirely original path forward for the modern creative.

At its heart, the project is a striking visual story about return, transformation, and the quiet courage required to be truly seen. Set against the vibrant, layered backdrop of Harlem, it follows a new generation of visionaries navigating the complex intersections of identity, survival, ambition, and community. Much like Dorothy’s journey down the yellow brick road, these artists eventually confront a universal truth: everything they have been searching for has existed within themselves, and within the community standing right beside them, all along.

The project is spearheaded by Harlem Labs, a multidisciplinary creative studio founded by Jamont Hanshaw that focuses on visual storytelling, creative direction, and collaborative artistry. For Hanshaw and the studio, this effort reflects the chaotic, beautiful reality of “creating while becoming.” It emphasizes the desperate need for spaces where emerging and historically underrepresented artists do not just survive, but feel profoundly supported, visible, and free to experiment without restraint.

Far transcending a standard fashion story, the work serves as a cultural manifesto. It poses a fundamental question: what happens when artists stop waiting for institutional permission and simply start building worlds of their own?

By rootedness in ancestral pride and an unwavering belief in self-determination, Harlem Labs isn’t just capturing culture—it is expanding the boundaries of what becomes possible when community becomes the canvas.

items.title: A New Book Celebrates More Than 250 Trailblazing Women Photographers Across 200 Years
items.content:
A New Book Celebrates More Than 250 Trailblazing Women Photographers Across 200 Years

August 14, 2026
BooksHistoryPhotography
Jackie Andres
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

In the introduction of a new book titled Great Women Photographers, Fiona Rogers writes, “If ‘greatness’ has long been defined by visibility and remembrance, then the continued documentation and celebration of women’s photographic practice is not only relevant but essential.”

The forthcoming title spans a multitude of photographic works from 68 countries and covers nearly 200 years of history. It’s the fourth volume in Phaidon’s series of books commemorating influential women in the artistic sphere, with previous installments focusing on distinct creative mediums such as painting and sculpting.

Highlighting more than 250 women in the field of photography, Great Women Photographers is organized alphabetically by name. Each artist entry includes recently commissioned texts written by leading scholars, accompanied with iconic images from the featured photographers.

From photojournalism and editorial portraiture to cameraless images and conceptual landscapes, Great Women Photographers is not only a visual record of the diverse contributions made by women but also, as the publisher notes, “a new lens on the world, inviting readers to discover, engage with, and be inspired by the work of some of the world’s greatest image-makers.”

You may also enjoy exploring other titles in the series, including Great Women Artists, Great Women Painters, and Great Women Sculptors. Great Women Photographers is slated for release on October 14, 2026. Pre-order your copy in the Colossal Shop. We also have a copy of Great Women Sculptors available now.

items.title: Photographing Concerts and Live Events on Film by Angela Izzo
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Angela Izzo

Photographing a live event feels as though I’ve been transported back to the very place where my love for photography first took root—somewhere between the music, the people, and the electricity of live shows.

As someone who has always chased experiences, I found myself completely immersed in the world of music from as early as I can remember. I spent years traveling with bands, losing myself in venues, moving effortlessly between backstage, onstage, and the heart of the crowd. Every moment carried its own kind of magic, and every experience became part of the way I learned to see.

Long before I realized it, those nights were shaping not only my perspective but also the eye I would eventually bring to photography. Looking back now, it all feels like living inside the film Almost Famous—a life measured by songs, stories, and the beautiful chaos that exists between them.

An Unexpected Film Camera for Live Events and Concerts

Looking back through these concert images—some taken more than a decade ago—I’m reminded of what I love most about photography: its ability to preserve a moment that can never be recreated. These photographs are more than documentation of a performance; they’re fragments of a feeling, a time, and a place.

While I was always drawn to the energy onstage, I found myself equally captivated by the people in the crowd—the friends, the strangers, and the quiet moments unfolding between songs.

Although I often carried professional digital cameras, I almost always had my tiny Diana Mini with a flash tucked away. That little camera captured a kind of magic the larger equipment never could.

Small enough to slip into any venue, it invited curiosity instead of intimidation. People would light up when they saw it, letting their guard down in a way they rarely did in front of a larger camera. Those unguarded moments became some of my favorite photographs.

As a professional photographer, I often carried large camera bodies and lenses—gear that required credentials and full press access to get where I needed to be. But when I wanted to move through the night more casually and capture moments without drawing attention, I always reached for a small film camera. I’d choose just one to carry, keeping things light for the long haul.

The Diana Mini quickly became a favorite. With up to 72 frames on a single roll, it allowed me to document an entire night in a fluid, spontaneous way. It wasn’t about technical perfection—it was about preserving the energy, the movement, and the moments.

The Benefits of a Small Camera

Many of the shows I photograph are ones where I’m invited by the band or already know the artists, which gives me the opportunity to arrive early and spend time backstage. Those moments become my favorite photographs.

In those settings, a small film camera is an advantage. In my experience, it’s far less intimidating to security, venue staff, and the people around me than a full professional digital setup.

The moment you walk in with large cameras and lenses, you’re more likely to be stopped, questioned, or asked for credentials. But with a compact film camera, I can move through the space more naturally. I can blend into the crowd, experience the show as a guest, and capture authentic moments as they unfold.

Related: Diana Mini Camera Review

Choosing a Film Stock That Matches the Event

One of the most important considerations when shooting film is choosing the right ISO for the environment.

If I’m photographing outdoors during the day, I can usually shoot without a flash using a film stock rated between ISO 100 and 400. But when the light starts to fade—or I’m shooting indoors at a concert or event—I reach for ISO 400 to 800 film and switch on my flash. That combination gives me the flexibility to embrace the atmosphere while still capturing the energy and spontaneity of the moment.

Choosing a film stock comes down to the look and feeling you want to create. For my documentary-style approach, I like to keep things simple with a 35mm color film at ISO 400. It’s versatile enough to handle most concert environments while staying true to the moment.

If you’re looking to experiment, though, film offers endless creative possibilities. You can play with different color palettes, specialty film stocks, or embrace more abstract, unpredictable results. I’ve even photographed shows with a Polaroid camera. It’s certainly bulkier to carry than a compact film camera, but awesome for that instant gratification. Makes it well worth the extra space in my bag.

Getting Close to the Action

Photographing artists onstage with a film camera can be more challenging than shooting digitally. Depending on the lens you’re using, your images may lean toward a softer focus, or you may not be close enough to capture the moment the way you envision it. That’s part of the unpredictability—and the charm—of shooting film.

When I’m photographing in a smaller venue, though, everything changes. Being able to stand onstage or just a few feet from the artists makes it much easier to create intimate, dynamic images. That proximity allows me to capture not only the performance itself but also the connection between the musicians and the audience in a way that feels immediate and personal.

Capturing the Atmosphere

One of my favorite parts of photographing live shows is capturing the atmosphere beyond the stage. I’m drawn to the people just as much as the performers—their style, their energy, and the way they express themselves, especially when a show has a theme. The audience is part of the story, and I love documenting the personalities that make each event unique.

Whenever I see someone whose look catches my eye, I’ll stop and ask, “Can I take your photo?” More often than not, they’re excited to say yes. I think there’s something disarming about holding a small film camera or a Polaroid. It feels less like paparazzi and more like an invitation to create something together.

Those nostalgic cameras encourage people to let their guard down, making it easier to capture an honest portrait that reflects who they are in that moment.

Using Creative Techniques

When I’m photographing events, I love experimenting with techniques that push beyond documenting the moment. Double exposures and prisms are some of my favorite creative tools, adding a surreal, dreamlike quality that echoes the energy of live music.

Whether I’m shooting Polaroids or 35mm film, I always embrace the pop of an on-camera flash. It gives the images a raw, documentary feel. With cameras like my Diana, I can layer exposures and create soft, overlapping frames that exaggerate motion and atmosphere.

Sometimes, I’ll pair those techniques with an experimental film stock, introducing bold colors or  textures that add another layer of personality to the photograph. 

Final Thoughts

My biggest piece of advice is to stay present and truly observe your surroundings. It’s easy to get caught up in the chaos of a show, but sometimes the best photographs come when you step away from it.

If the crowd feels overwhelming, move to a different corner of the venue or look for a new perspective. Changing your point of view can completely transform the story you’re telling. Every concert or live event has countless stories unfolding at once—the magic lies in discovering the one that speaks to you.

Whenever I have a camera in my hands, a sense of calm settles over me. It’s almost meditative. My camera becomes an extension of myself—my brush, my eye, and at times, my shield.

Through the viewfinder, I become completely immersed in the world around me, searching for the details that others might overlook: the light or a gesture, the movement of the crowd, or a quiet moment between the noise. Those are the pieces that come together to tell a story.

items.title: Gold-tinged togetherness as Londoners flock to Primrose Hill for the solar eclipse
items.excerpt: Celestial gathering — Ella Glossop photographs the once in decades event from one the city’s most popular gathering spots, and the community spirit that encapsulated the moment. London hasn’t seen a solar eclipse this
items.content:
Celestial gathering — Ella Glossop photographs the once in decades event from one the city’s most popular gathering spots, and the community spirit that encapsulated the moment.

London hasn’t seen a solar eclipse this big since 1999.

Now in the big year or 2026, as thousands flock to the peak of Primrose Hill for the spectacle, there’s still something ’90s about it. Maybe it’s DIY-ness of all the tech: Meta glasses aren’t going to cut it here, so it’s holographic plastic lenses on cardboard straps. Phone cameras aren’t any good at picturing the sun, so people have brought different camera set ups, colanders, cereal-box projectors. Maybe it’s the fact that - during the day in summer - it’s not 35 degrees. Maybe, as the sun sets behind the moon and the light flattens, it’s the weird feeling that things might be okay.

A two-hour long affair – the eclipse reached its peak at 7:13PM, where over 90% of the sun is covered. We won’t see coverage this full again until 2081. The moment draws a big cheer from the crowd – who are huddled shoulder-to-shoulder on picnic rugs, with bottles of fizz popping and boom boxes pumping tunes. Then, as the sun emerges from behind the moon and normal daylight resumes, it’s hazy like it as at 5am.

  • Read next: Danny León pulls huge aerial in line with the solar eclipse

The modern world is fraught, big tech is big, the internet is loud – and once every few decades, we get a cosmic-sanctioned dose of perspective.

Huck’s Ella Glossop was there to capture the scenes. See her photographs below.

items.title: ‘Turn the Volume Up!’ Highlights the History of Speaking Out for Change in America
items.content:
‘Turn the Volume Up!’ Highlights the History of Speaking Out for Change in America

August 13, 2026
ArtHistoryPhotographySocial Issues
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

From the collection of the Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University, which features a wealth of artwork and artifacts related to social justice and community organizing, a new exhibition highlights American democracy and freedom of speech through the lens of art as an agent of change.

Turn the volume up! includes works by a diverse group of contemporary artists and photographers, from Spider Martin’s dramatic documentation of Freedom Marches during the Civil Rights Movement to Kara Walker’s multimedia interrogations of U.S. history and racial stereotypes. Visitors will also encounter works by the Guerilla Girls, Carrie Mae Weems, Kiki Smith, Bruce Davidson, and many more.

The Nasher has organized the exhibition into five thematic areas: Remarks, Organize, Records, Dissents, and Petitions. Photographs, sculptures, installations, paintings, and more illustrate the array of visual languages artists use to convey important messages, influencing how people discuss issues and are spurred toward civic action.

The Guerilla Girls, for example, famously pasted posters around Manhattan in the 1980s that shone a light on the glaring lack of representation of women artists in not only visual art but across popular culture. Davidson is renowned for illuminating social inequality in visceral photographs, from the Jim Crow South to impoverished neighborhoods in New York City. And Carol Summers’ bold screenprint of a giant red “X” over a photo of a Vietnamese mother and her children was part of a campaign by Artists and Writers Protest urging the end of the war in Vietnam.

Throughout the show’s run, pieces will be rotated in and out so that visitors can experience a wide array of works in the museum’s collection. Turn the volume up! opens on August 27 and will continue through July 11, 2027. Everything Now All at Once also continues through November 1.

items.title: The Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalists Highlight the Sorrowful and Sublime
items.content:
The Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalists Highlight the Sorrowful and Sublime

August 13, 2026
NaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Our oceans are places of mystery and biological wonders as much as they are essential to communities’ livelihoods. We tap these expansive bodies of water for recreation, food, transportation. From the Atlantic to the Arctic, oceans cover around 70 percent of the earth’s surface, and there is an incredible wealth of life yet to be discovered.

As the continuing climate crisis melts ice caps and raises sea levels, and industrial fishing and waste threatens endangered marine animals and habitats, reminders of the oceans’ irreplaceable value and power are ever more critical. That’s where Oceanographic magazine and Blancpain’s annual Ocean Photographer of the Year contest comes in as a catalyst for conservation.

This year’s finalists span categories from Adventure and Human Connection to Ocean Unseen and Conservation. To really delve into the complexity of issues facing our saltwater expanses, the latter is organized in two parts: Hope and Impact. Throughout, there is a sense that in order for people to really become aware of the problems facing our oceans, let alone feel motivated to act, we need to understand both the beauty and the terribleness of these waters, whether inherent or human-inflicted.

Founder and director Will Harrison describes the contest as a platform for stories to reach the world. “These photographs don’t just capture what’s beneath the surface; they surface the stories our planet most needs us to hear. As the pressures on our ocean grow, so does the importance of the artists who bear witness to them.”

The winners will be announced in September. See all the finalists in the competition’s online gallery, and follow updates on Instagram.

items.title: Jennifer Latour Preserves Ephemeral Beauty in Her Otherworldly Botanical Assemblages
items.content:
Jennifer Latour Preserves Ephemeral Beauty in Her Otherworldly Botanical Assemblages

August 12, 2026
ArtNaturePhotography
Grace Ebert
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

“The wind is my nemesis!” says Jennifer Latour, and rightly so. In her sculptural assemblages, single flowers or small clusters of blooms sprout from tree branches or thick stems, appearing like otherworldly forms standing in the landscape. A soft breeze could topple the Vancouver-based artist’s ephemeral works, scattering their delicate petals and spindly shoots before she has the chance to snap a photo.

These fleeting moments are preserved in Latour’s Bound Species series, which she began during lockdown by piecing together objects found around her home into unconventional, ikebana-style compositions. “During this time, I started having a recurring dream of giant flowers growing around me with multiple species of other flowers growing off one stem. I draw a lot of inspiration from my dreams, and this was something I had to test out in real life,” she tells us.

After a few trials, the process clicked. She ideated on the ways different colors and shapes might puzzle together into a sort of hybrid character and envisioned photographing on location, presenting the unorthodox arrangements in stunning, natural settings. When travel became possible, she jumped at the opportunity to bring the sculptures outdoors. That’s when she encountered the wind. “I quickly discovered how much more difficult this was,” she says. “It takes so much more patience and time to make my sculptures out in the wild but all that much more satisfying when it works out!”

Today, Latour continues to venture outdoors and often sources materials from local garden centers, flower shops, and even the occasional grocery store, should the botanicals be locally grown. She assembles each piece by hand, connecting stem to stem in a way that evokes “the interconnectedness found in nature, and serves as a reminder that all creatures are bound simultaneously by both their similarities and their differences.”

With trips planned to Arizona and the U.K. seaside in the coming months, the artist will continue to transform colorful specimens into strange, mishmashed forms. “I dream of taking the work all around the world to the most remote and unique locations,” she adds. “It’s a practice I see myself continuing to create and evolve until either my hands or my body stop working.”

Latour’s images are currently on view in two group exhibitions—Where the Seasons Endure at Gallery COA in Montreal and The House and the Forest at Can Balaguer in Palma, Mallorca—and she’s also planning for a solo show in 2027. Keep up with her travels and projects on Instagram.

items.title: Harman Phoenix has a new look – and a new ISO
items.content:
Harman Technology is reducing the price of its Harman Photo-branded colour negative films and re-releasing the original Phoenix film with an important update.

The repackaged Harman Phoenix will no longer be an ISO 200 film but will be DX coded for ISO 125.

Harman Technology said it had repackaged the film after feedback from photographers who said the film responded better to being shot at a lower ISO.

The new listing on the Harman Photo shop reads:  “Harman Phoenix 125 retains the same characteristics that you loved (or hated) about the original but with a new speed of 125 to reflect how you told us you shoot it.”

According to Harman Technology, the film still shows high contrast and strong, visible grain at this lower ISO, and should be shot accordingly.

It also says that it can be developed in E6 or ECN-2 chemicals as well.

The listing says: “With a DX coded cassette and a box speed of ISO 125, It performs best in good, consistent light and on brighter days or when shooting into the light there is also a possibility of halation.

‘It delivers punchy, vibrant colours although they react differently to different scanners and settings. Getting the exposure right will certainly help to get the best results so we suggest metering for the mid tones to retain shadow or highlight detail (over or under exposure is not Phoenix’s friend)!”

While the price of the new version of the film – also available in 120 – has not yet been made public, film is expected to be available from stockists as early as next week.

Meanwhile, other films such as Phoenix’s follow-up Phoenix II has been reduced in price to just £7.32 in the UK for a 24-shot roll and £9.27 for a 36-frame roll, with further reductions for five-packs and 10-packs of film. The price of 120 film is also being reduced to £7.90 a roll.

Harman Photo’s experimental films, Red and the recently released Switch Azure, are also seeing price reductions.

items.title: Gazing Through Chaos: Italo Calvino, seashells, and a conversation with Charles Negre
items.content:
Certain sensibilities are necessary not only for what they reveal about the era in which they belong, but because their influence extends far beyond their physical presence in the world. In this sense, Italo Calvino was a forerunner of something that is now glaringly obvious: we are increasingly unable to find points of reference within ourselves, a sense of balance, a verticality; we have forgotten the strategies to do so and have fewer and fewer resources to go back and seek them out.

Italo Calvino had a special relationship with the tangible world. Always divided, indecisive, a soul torn between two worlds: the real world and the other world—that is, the world of thought, of the words used to describe it. Italo Calvino, poor restless soul, was probably incapable of performing simple actions without thinking—leaving the house, taking a stroll, going to the sea, walking on the sand, watching the waves and the seagulls—he was unable to be satisfied with what he saw or heard. Within him burned the fire of something greater, like an impulse, a desire for a deeper connection with things.

In this sense, the sea was Calvino’s absolute destination of choice; the sea as an open theater, infinite by definition, a stage for his endless thoughts.

A young Italo Calvino wrote in a letter to Natalia Ginzburg that, having returned one day to his hometown of Sanremo to dispel the confusion of a reality he already found too touristy and teeming, and to regain his concentration, he began to draw, trying to copy some shells found in an old collection. The results were not masterpieces of the visual arts, but they were enough to quiet the chaos.

The practice, linked to close observation, to the meticulous search for details of form and color, linked to the hand, to the mark, to the tangible object, can become a way to create transparent walls around oneself, like a portable room where the goal is not to exclude oneself from reality, but to rediscover a center, to recalibrate, and then return to the outside world without succumbing to it.

The shell, in and of itself, is not a neutral entity: to use Calvino’s words, we might say that the shell is the singularity that contains multiplicity. A shell is a bridge between two universes, a primordial creature motionless yet alive, an ancient microcosm that lingers as a testament to what once was. In a tale from Cosmicomics, Italo Calvino has his protagonist—a creature that has travelled through the history of the universe—take the form of a mollusk, which, in an attempt to connect with its absolute aspiration for universal love, constructs its own shell, just as a sculptor builds his masterpiece. Through him, we discover that shells and the mollusks that inhabit them are blind creatures, and the marvel of their form is the result of their profound, intimate, and ancestral striving toward an unconditional desire for beauty—a desire that, however, can only acquire meaning through the eyes of those whom evolution has endowed with sight. It is, in other words, a gift they have provided for us.

Charles Negre is a French photographer, born in 1988 and working in Paris, whose practice spans between editorial and commercial photography as well as personal and artistic research. After graduating from the renowned ÉCAL, he has collaborated with leading contemporary fashion magazines and brands, in addition to personal projects with independent publishing houses. His work focuses primarily on studio photography and the still-life genre, which he continually reinterprets, moving in parallel with contemporary demands and the medium’s evolution, navigating the space between reality and construction. Furthermore, he explores the interplay between commissioned work and personal research, creating an extremely cohesive and consistent body of work. The Shells series engages with aesthetic elements characteristic of early still-life photography and plays with the ambiguity of familiar shapes; this retelling of a common object also encapsulates a fascination with the recurring patterns found in the symmetries inherent to natural elements.

Charles Negre’s shells are an exercise of the gaze, the final act of an exploration of form as a bridge between worlds. Through close observation and subsequent abstraction, the everyday transcends its own boundaries and appears in its most essential essence, as pure form, not as an empty vessel, but as a shifting structure. These forms are what remains beyond meaning, the unconditional beauty of which Calvino spoke.

This can only happen because, in Charles Negre’s images, objects hold absolute prominence; they appear, more than ever, in their material dimension, revealed through the attention devoted to roughness, which brings the sense of touch to the forefront. It is precisely the surfaces that serve as the space where their meaning is inscribed; the surface, in fact, is not to be understood as a mere container and physical appearance, but as a living space through which the outside and the inside can communicate—it’s the epidermis of things, vulnerable and sensitive. Calvino himself maintained that it is precisely through the surface of things that a profound knowledge of them becomes possible—or rather, that access to the infinity of meanings becomes possible.

So then, what is the relationship between Calvino’s drawings and the images we create today? When we talk about rediscovering a connection with things, what role do images play? Can we truly experience reality by observing it?

There is a knot that forms between the real, the tangible, and the gaze, and we are called upon to untangle it—or perhaps not to untangle it, but to recognize it. Perhaps, to truly “touch” things, we only need to rise above, pause, and look. Drawings, like photographs, and thus images in general, can serve as an exercise or a tool to grapple with the elusiveness of things and to escape the never-ending chaos of reality.

And while it is true that we must recognize the limits of our present, which carries us ever further away from material things and ever closer to their representations, at the same time we cannot resign ourselves to the idea that all is lost, because the tangible world is still here before us, doing nothing but reflecting us as we look at it. What we must do is learn to recognize it again.

Charles Negre: Still-life is actually all about that: stillness and slowing down the time to observe and document.

Marta Valdegrani: In the article, I compare your images from the Shells series with Italo Calvino’s drawings, and my conclusion is that maybe they are actually the same thing, in terms of process. To really touch reality, to be in contact with reality, it all comes through the gaze, through the act of looking; by making time to look at things in a different way.

C.N.: I think it’s about choosing to spend time to try to look at things with care. And once you take that time, then you start seeing things in mundane objects or random objects—some sort of spectacularity or specificity that makes objects look suddenly special. Shells are already spectacular, but in a way, everyone knows what a shell looks like. Only once you start looking closely can you begin to see a lot of elements in there. And I have the feeling that the pastas, in a way, are similar. One thing that is a bit funny is that they’re also artificial, they’re man-made, and they’re done by factories, but at the same time, this doesn’t take out some of the poetry that they carry, and their materiality. Our brain creates connections so that we have the feeling that the object is natural, but it’s not natural at all; we’re just looking at organic shapes and forms that kind of relate to our brain. So that’s quite a funny and interesting process.

M.V.: I also think that different things, even the most mundane things, have this sort of inner research for beauty, even though it doesn’t serve anything. Everything goes towards that ideal of beauty.

C.N.: There’s no hierarchy in beauty, in the sense that a beautiful piece of jewelry is just a beautiful piece of jewelry, and a beautiful piece of pasta by itself is something that could be looked at, and that can also be found beautiful. It’s just a matter of choosing what’s beautiful or not. And then with the help of photography, you can really translate it and use the light to highlight these natural connections that you see. It’s about using photography as a sort of witness to this thing.

M.V.: So if I interpret this correctly, maybe you would say there is no difference between a more mundane object and a more precious one?

C.N.: I think the concept of preciousness is really subjective; the things that someone could find precious are a result of their subjectivity. At work and at my place you could find many different objects, and one could be a really normal and uninteresting coffee cup, like a paper cup, but it could have a particular shape that is nice to look at or something written on it that is really funny, and it’s as important as something really nicely crafted. I think that it’s important to say that, depending on how you look at them, you can really find the beauty in these little objects.

M.V.: I think this is really evident mostly from your work that comes from commissions, but I can say for sure that it’s visible, maybe in a quieter way, also in your personal work. So, given that for you there is no hierarchy, I was wondering what your perception of the relationship between photography and reality is.

C.N.: Well, I think photography is a tool to look at reality. The photographer sees things and photography is a language to then show that to others. I use photography as a tool to witness nature and the world that surrounds us, and I only focus on objects and still objects because I feel they’re more honest, in a way. You see, objects can’t lie. In a way, it’s harder to find a way to photograph them than people. I take pictures of animals sometimes, but I think people are so complicated, because they come with a background; they come with a personality, and with so many things that you can have no other grip on. So, I feel like what comes out is not really honest. Whereas, if you shoot an apple, then an apple is an apple, and it’s the way you are going to photograph it that is going to make it special.

M.V.: And maybe with objects you, as the photographer, are able to become the subject of the picture in a more direct way.

C.N.: Of course, because once you start photographing objects, you are the mastermind behind the objects and you can create languages and conversations between them, which is a really important aspect and it’s also infinite; there are endless possibilities with it.

M.V.: So we could say that in the same way Calvino was drawing shells, maybe photography is your tool to find balance.

C.N.: Yes, I think so. Personally, I’ve never stopped making pictures. I’ve always photographed and I cannot stop doing it. It’s really complicated, I do it almost compulsively. Every time I find a new idea, maybe I don’t photograph it, but I keep the idea in my head, I draw it, I hold it there, because I know it could be a good photograph. I use photography as an everyday act, to just document the things I see, document the things I want to stage. To relate to what Calvino said, to me, photography is definitely a sort of therapy. Photography is really a way of looking at the world, and I think drawing is the same thing, the act of composing, making mental images. What I do is, I have a mental image that I want to try to recreate, and I let reality be involved in the process.

M.V.: Maybe a photograph doesn’t have inherent meaning, but the meaning comes through the effort that you make to capture reality.

C.N.: Exactly. And what’s really nice about photography, and maybe sometimes a bit frustrating with drawing, for example, is that with photography you have many parameters and tools you can use to build up your idea and your emotions. Composition, framing, light, it’s really highly technical, but all this technique helps you get to the idea you have in your mind. Some people get anxious in front of a white empty studio because it means having endless possibilities, but personally, I get excited because once I do one day of shooting in the studio, I know that I can spend another twenty years doing it and it always will be different because of those possibilities. I understand the stress of looking at an empty space, and I guess it’s the same thing with the white blank page for a writer, but there’s something so exciting about the idea of creating a world, of creating a conversation between objects that only lasts for a short period of time, and then it’s gone. I feel like people often think, for example with cinema, that emotions only come through character and people and life struggle and drama; but I think you can have a lot of drama through objects, a lot of emotions there. It’s just that as a photographer you have to be really subtle with your own emotions to be able to show that. For example, maybe that spider on your notebook could create a sort of strange emotion, or the image of a liquid in a bed could create a reminiscence. All these things can strike a chord in your brain.

M.V.: I think that your images offer a lot of room for interpretation, not in the sense that they force an interpretation, but they offer many ways in which they can make you feel. I have one last question and I don’t know if there’s an answer, really, but I know that shells are a recurring theme for you, because I read that, in addition to this series, you have a lot more pictures of actual shells in your archive. So I was wondering if, for you, there’s a memory or an emotion linked to this object.

C.N.: I think shells are highly symbolic. They have been a recurring image in history: the image of the shell was already present in early Dutch paintings. It’s the first thing you bring back from holidays as a kid, and one of the first things adventurers came back with, in the 16th century, from all over the world. But what I find mostly interesting is not really the real shell—I do have some real shells, and I do take photographs of them. But what I love most is calling a shell something that is not a shell. Let’s say that pasta is a shell; but the coffee cup that is left in a sewer or on the street is also a shell of some sort—a leftover. A shell is all the things that are a capsule of something else, and that you can’t use anymore. They’re just leftovers of recipients of something. All these things look like shells to me. I think shells also hold many layers of time. They’re like the circles inside trees, that once you cut them, you can go through time. They were also recipients of life, because every shell was an animal. The animal is now gone, and the shell is what is left. And maybe, also, a future recipient of something else.
