items.title: Suzanne Jongmans Recycles Everyday Materials for Elegant Renaissance-Style Portraits
items.content:
Suzanne Jongmans Recycles Everyday Materials for Elegant Renaissance-Style Portraits

August 12, 2026
ArtPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

From materials we normally discard like padded packaging or the mesh sleeves that protect fruit from bruising, Suzanne Jongmans summons elegant and dreamlike Renaissance portraits.

The artist drapes models in lush velvet fabrics and typically positions them against deep backgrounds in the vein of Leonardo da Vinci’s “Lady with an Ermine” (1489-91) or Antonello da Messina’s “Portrait of a Young Man” (c. 1470). The settings and the addition of fine garments contrast found plastic detritus with hints of refinement and the figures’ dignified postures, mirroring the solemn, pious expressions of individuals in Renaissance portraiture. Recently, she has also incorporated copper coils extracted from the electric motors of disused household appliances and fuses.

Jongmans infuses her works with nods to gender roles and issues that still raise the hackles of “polite society,” such as breastfeeding in public. The artist seamlessly ties a centuries-old aesthetic to salient contemporary concerns, exploring femininity, individuality, and the nature of concealment. Through the latter especially, she delves into the human capacity for wonder and its significance at a time when technology, the gears of so-called progress, and revisionism endanger our connections to the natural world, our histories, and one another.

The artist describes her approach as an exploration of the space between the material and the immaterial world, one where society, eras, emotions, and cosmic forces converge. “Since the Enlightenment, reason has been glorified and the Western tendency towards a drive for modernization and mechanization has increased,” Jongmans says in a statement. “The significance of myths and imagination in our daily lives seems to have been lost or at least faded into the background.”

By exploring the past, Jongmans creates exquisitely contemporary compositions, prompting us to consider the meaning of value and how it is assigned. The works are also sensitive, introspective meditations on human feeling, and she has even occasionally turned the camera on herself. “In the Midst of It All,” for example, is a self-portrait taken during the pandemic that serves as a reminder to slow down, rest, and reconnect not only with the surrounding environment but with oneself.

See more on Jongmans’ Instagram.

items.title: Get Up Close to the Sun in the Highest Resolution Image Ever Captured
items.content:
Get Up Close to the Sun in the Highest Resolution Image Ever Captured

August 12, 2026
PhotographyScience
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Scientists have long studied how magnetic energy powers solar activity. The constant motion of plasma particles and the sun’s rotation are major contributors to its cycles and events, such as flares and coronal mass ejections, which lob huge quantities of plasma and gas into space.

Sometimes these explosions reach the earth’s magnetic field and cause geomagnetic storms, which are when we see some of the most brilliant auroras. But they also disrupt or damage our communications systems, power grids, GPS, and satellites. Researchers want to further understand how the sun builds up its magnetic energy so we better know how to guard against its massive fits of activity. They’ve also been trying to figure out why the sun’s corona, or atmosphere, is millions of degrees hotter than its surface.

Thanks to the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which has pride of place at the National Solar Observatory on Maui, Hawaii, the highest-resolution image of the sun ever captured has revealed unique features that may give solar scientists some insight into how this magnetic energy builds.

Rippling forms that physicists call Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability (KHI) demonstrate the effect of two fluids flowing past each other at different velocities. It’s a phenomenon named for the two scientists who observed it for the first time around 1870, and it can be seen in clouds, ocean waves, and the atmospheres of gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn.

The Inouye telescope, the most powerful of its kind, was able to capture features smaller than 12 miles across, providing insights that remained hidden in earlier photos. The details may illuminate part of a solar process that scientists refer to as “flux braiding,” so named because of the way the sun’s magnetic field lines move around one another result in a plaited effect. The tension builds and builds before eventually breaking, which is when we see flares and similar events. The swirls of KHI may have something to do with how these twists happen in the first place.

“This could solve this biggest mystery of the last half a century for solar physics and astrophysics,” team scientist Dr. David Kuridze told The Guardian. “When you have this instability in the system, it is very easy to cascade the energy into smaller scales. And at some point, it just dissipates as a heat. This could make hot coronas, hot outer atmospheres of the sun and similar stars.”

items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Today, we’re featuring a lovely photo series from film photographer Ausra Linkeviciute. Here is more from Ausra about photographing Highgate Cemetery…

Highgate cemetery in North London has long been a place I loved to visit and photograph. And yet, having photographed it before with my digital cameras, something was always missing – the depth and richness of that green color, the peacefulness, stillness, and mystery of the place… This time I ventured out with my new Mamiya, still with the excitement of just learning to use it. At one moment, I came across an incredible scene tucked away in the corner above all the crypts. There was a white carpet of petals under the tree with a doorframe in the background, and in the light breeze, more petals were still falling. I spent a long while at this spot, and instead of snapping away on my DSLR (had I brought it), I took just two images. This time, I knew this was finally the right camera, as looking at the final image I felt all the same emotions I did when standing there. That to me is the power of film I am in the process of discovering – this ability to bring back a physical trace and the emotion of the place we are capturing.

items.title: Surveying community and resistance in LGBTQ+ nightlife
items.excerpt: Sex, Clubs Dissent — A new book collates queer nightlife photography over the past 50 years, and the people who found refuge and safe spaces after dark. For over a century, queer nightlife thrived in the margins of soc
items.content:
Sex, Clubs Dissent — A new book collates queer nightlife photography over the past 50 years, and the people who found refuge and safe spaces after dark.

For over a century, queer nightlife thrived in the margins of society, driven underground by the criminalisation of sexuality and genders beyond the binary. Here in bars, clubs, ballrooms, warehouses, bathhouses, dungeons, cruising grounds, and strolls where sex is sold, generations have come together as an act of love and resistance against a world that shunned them. In those clandestine spaces, queer culture took root, becoming the lingua franca of music, style, beauty, glamour, and attitude – to say nothing of political activism and mutual aid that has saved lives and changed laws. 

Progress, however, can be a double-edged sword with the price of conditional freedom being cultural appropriation by a mainstream all too willing to erase the source. Ballroom colloquialisms like ‘the tea’, ‘kiki’, ‘shade’, ‘slay’, ‘reading’, ‘gagging’, and ‘giving’ are often mislabelled as ‘gen Z slang’ while contemporary and historic Black, brown and LGBTQ+ creators are paid dust. 

“There’s an acceleration of ubiquitous hyper capitalism and absorption of queer culture,” says author Amelia Abraham, on the phone from the streets of London. She’s just had a pop into The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop, where her latest book, Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife (MACK), is set among the new arrivals. The book’s red cover beckons with a keyhole glimpse of unbridled amour, revealed to be Meryl Meisler’s photograph of two women on the floor of Les Mouches, a members-only queer nightclub on Manhattan’s west side in the late 1970s. It’s a delectable promise of things to come. 

  • Read next: Inside Parkuir: the art project queering sport, space and our bodies

In Sex, Clubs, Dissent, Abraham explores the intersections of community, creativity, desire, and liberation, spotlighting the originators and innovators who blazed their own paths over half a century. Bringing together the work of artists including David Wojnarowicz, Sunil Gupta, Mariette Pathy Allen, Bruce LaBruce, Reynaldo Rivera, Linda Simpson, Lyle Ashton Harris, Clifford Prince King, and Chloe Sherman, the book is a panoramic landscape of the power and pride that’s only found when the night comes alive. 

Although Abraham started clubbing as a teen, it wasn’t until she discovered The Joiners Arms at the age of 21 that she finally had a place to call her own. “It was really chaotic. The floor was sticky with beer, the toilets were flooded, and it felt lawless and exciting to me,” she remembers fondly of the fabled Shoreditch dive bar. “It was loads of people from different subcultures coming together, a real melting pot, like the 60-year-old trans matriarch Stephanie, who always sat at the bar. It was one of the first places where I really fell in love with queer nightlife.” 

Drawn to the intergenerational aspect of Joiners, Abraham struck up a friendship with photographer Jeffrey Hinton, whose portrait of dancer Michael Clark, appears in the book. “Jeff is in his 60s and I’ve had the pleasure of hearing his stories about the nightlife that came before,” she says. “He has the same kind of attitude that Joiners had, which is quite DIY, egalitarian, and messy. That’s what we’re talking about with the word ‘dissent’ – a kind of disorderliness. Fuck it! Just do it – and do it for the love of it!” 

  • Read next: An intimate window into New York’s ’70s lesbian scene

It is this ethos that Abraham brings to the book, crafting a tour de force that is as much a photographic history as it is a family album, particularly in light of the criminalisation of queer sexuality around the globe. “The Gay Rights Movement started with visibility. Before that, the camera was dangerous,” she says. “Photographers from that time talk about how they couldn’t show their photos because someone might lose their job or their family. And that’s true for now for certain people.”

Sex, Clubs, Dissent: Visualising Queer Nightlife (2026) by Amelia Abraham published by MACK. It will have its US launch on September 8, 2026, at the Leslie-Lohman Museum of Art in New York.

items.title: Video of The Week: Why Do It?
items.content:
The film originated as David Fiene’s idea, born when he pointed a camera and asked a question that proved surprisingly difficult to answer properly throughout the entire shoot. Over the years, many explanations had been offered for why someone would choose to rise early to run, endure leg kicks that leave them unable to walk properly for days, or repeatedly return to a room where their shortcomings are laid bare, but most of those responses were merely convenient enough to end a conversation rather than reveal a fundamental truth.

Originally a secondary school mathematics teacher from New York who moved to Barcelona roughly nine years ago, she stumbled into Muay Thai almost by accident under the instruction of Pablo Rayo, having never considered herself an athlete nor searching for a sport. Like many women, she had survived sexual and domestic violence, responding by firmly deciding that anger was not the answer after seeing the destruction it could cause. Believing violence was never a solution, she kept her emotions hidden away and assumed she was fine, but Muay Thai stripped away that illusion not through mysticism, but through raw, visible struggle.

Being placed in situations where weakness, fatigue, and being out of one’s depth are exposed in front of others breaks through the surface, uncovering buried pain and leaving only the physical realization of whether one can fight back. Crucially, martial arts highlights the profound difference between pain inflicted without consent and pain that is willingly agreed to, where choosing the room, the partner, and the intensity allows the body to gradually relearn that it belongs to itself as the nervous system updates with new evidence. The genuine reason for continuing is not discipline, fitness, or enjoyment, but rather the reality that the pain is chosen, accompanied by a physical strength that contrasts sharply with past periods of powerlessness. This experience extends beyond any single individual or gender, speaking to anyone who has felt small or stripped of agency through illness, demanding work, grief, or immigration challenges, though women face an added societal expectation to take up less space and absorb impact rather than push back.

While hitting a pad for the first time often feels awkward or apologetic, consistent practice builds a presence that carries over into everyday life, prompting the co-founding of SOMA alongside Sevda Tunaboylu and Verena Walther to run free Muay Thai programs for migrant and refugee women in Barcelona. Clinical measurements consistently show meaningful improvements in wellbeing after every program cycle, yet the most convincing evidence remains watching participants realize they are allowed to stand their ground and be loud. Ultimately, the film offers no clean resolution to the central question, reflecting the reality that anyone claiming absolute certainty about enduring such repetitive discomfort is likely selling something, whereas the true significance lies simply in the ongoing act of choosing to step back into the room.

items.title: The Shifting Shapes of Self: Social Roles and Adaptability
items.content:
In modern society, identity is rarely a fixed or singular entity. Instead, we exist in a state of constant metamorphosis, continually reshaping ourselves to navigate the complex social roles we inhabit. We shift effortlessly—and sometimes painfully—between the professional, the familial, the vulnerable, and the rebellious. The Shifting Shapes of Self is a conceptual photographic series that captures this exact human fluidity, exploring how we adapt to the expectations of the environments around us.

Central to this visual exploration is Polina, who embodies four distinct archetypes within the series, each representing a different facet of the human experience. As the Saint Witch, she stands as a paradoxical figure blending the sacred and the forbidden, representing the tension between societal morality, innate wisdom, and hidden power.

In contrast, her portrayal of the Young Girl offers a portrait of innocence, raw vulnerability, and the unburdened curiosity that exists before the weight of external expectations takes hold. She then shifts into the Ambitious Prince, an embodiment of drive, authority, and rebellious agency that captures the hunger to conquer one’s circumstances and claim a place in the world. Finally, as the Person, she is stripped of all theatrical archetypes, grounding the series in raw, everyday humanity—the quiet, unmasked core that remains when all social performances fade away.

Through these contrasting personas, The Shifting Shapes of Self serves as both a mirror and a question. It asks where performance ends and authenticity begins, inviting viewers to reflect on the masks they wear, the roles they play, and the true nature of the self hidden beneath them all.

items.title: In photos: Electric nights in ’70s Japan
items.excerpt: Tokyo–Koza — Keizō Kitajima’s new photobook explores the explosion of party culture of Tokyo and Okinawa during an era of rapid change in the country, as well as its stranger turns. Photography emerged at the vanguard
items.content:
Tokyo–Koza — Keizō Kitajima’s new photobook explores the explosion of party culture of Tokyo and Okinawa during an era of rapid change in the country, as well as its stranger turns.

Photography emerged at the vanguard in Japan as the 1968–69 university protests signified the rise of the New Left amid a global revolution against Western imperialism. Liberated from the myth of “objectivity” and false hierarchies of form, a small group of Japanese artists and critics including Daidō Moriyama and Nakahira Takuma came together to create Provoke, a photography magazine that embraced the raw, radical, and expressionistic possibilities of the medium. 

Although Provoke only ran three issues, its legacy would inspire generations of photographers from around the globe, beginning with native son, Keizō Kitajima. “I began photography in the mid-1970s, around the time when the political fervour symbolised by the May 1968 Paris Uprising was beginning to subside,” he says. “At that time, photography was considered one of the most cutting-edge and powerful means of expression in Japan, and I was deeply impressed by it.” 

Born in 1954 in Suzaka, Nagano Prefecture, Kitajima first discovered the work of Nobuyoshi Araki and Daidō Moriyama as a teen, going on to study with the latter in 1975 at WORK SHOP Photography School, founded by members of Provoke after the magazine folded. The two established a lifelong collaboration that took root the following year with the creation of CAMP, an artist-run gallery, darkroom, and meeting space in the Shinjuku district of Tokyo. 

With Moriyama’s support, Kitajima began exploring Koza, the historical name for Okinawa City and second largest city on the island following Tokyo. “Okinawa has numerous US military bases, and Koza is a nightlife district catering to American soldiers,” Kitajima says. “When I frequented Koza, it was shortly after the Vietnam War, and the town was bustling with many returning soldiers. People from all over Southeast Asia gathered in Koza to do business with the American soldiers. Many of them, including the soldiers, carried painful experiences in their hearts. I heard a thousand sad stories and a hundred happy stories from them.” 

With the recent publication of Keizo Kitajima: Tokyo–Koza (Little Big Man Books), the artist returns to the start of his career, retracing a fascinating chapter of Japanese photography and history. The lush, oversize paperback brings together Kitajima’s early works, Photographs of Okinawa (1975–1979) and Tokyo 1979, to create an electric portrait of Japanese nightlife during the second half of the decade. 

In 1979, Kitajima mounted a monthly series of exhibitions at CAMP showcasing black and white photographs made around the gallery in Shinjuku Ni-chome, a former red light district, accompanied by booklets titled Photo Express: Tokyo. “Japan was undergoing rapid urbanisation, and I was fascinated by the image and energy of the city,” he says. “The city seemed like a chaotic entity where light and darkness coexisted. Wandering through the labyrinthine alleys of Tokyo, I sought an encounter with a truth that transcended good and evil.” 

Kitajima remembers the experience as a whirlwind, excitedly photographing people who frequented the area, delighting when they would come to exhibition openings when their images were hung. “I attempted to compress the act of shooting, production, and exhibition into a single act, presenting it with maximum volume,” he says. Kitajima transformed CAMP into a darkroom by covering the walls with rolls of photographic paper, projecting the negatives onto them, developing them with a sponge, rinsing them in a bucket of water, and opening the show the very next day in that state. 

It is only now, half a century after these two series were made, that they can be seen together as Kitajima always dreamed. “For me, there are no past photographs. All the photographs I take, including street photography, are in the present tense and reflect my current position,” he says. “I believe it’s important to repeatedly revisit the same photographs, and I continue to re-examine the photographs I’ve taken, reinterpreting them in new contexts. My photographs are always beyond me.”

Keizo Kitajima: Tokyo–Koza is published by Little Big Man Books.

items.title: ‘Remember Me’ Highlights Black Americans’ Self-Expression in Early Photography
items.content:
‘Remember Me’ Highlights Black Americans’ Self-Expression in Early Photography

August 10, 2026
HistoryPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

In our era of screens and proliferous imagery, it strains the imagination to comprehend a time before photography. Two centuries ago, an inventor named Nicéphore Niépce took the very first picture of his courtyard in France by fitting a pewter plate into a camera obscura. A few years later, a professional scene painter named Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre conceived of the aptly named daguerreotype, in which the image could be permanently fixed. He and Niépce both sold their technologies to the French government, which then published a how-to guide and facilitated the global spread of the process. In 1939, the first daguerrotypes were created in the U.S.

As they say, the rest is history. Except, we often only see a part of the whole story. Because the technology was expensive, and therefore having your photograph taken (let alone owning the equipment) was costly, the visual record of the 19th century in this medium is heavily skewed toward affluent, white individuals and families who could afford it. Due to the long exposure time required to capture the images, we also don’t see candid shots, as carefully posed scenes were required for clarity and fidelity.

Photography was invented decades before the Civil War and the end of slavery in the U.S., yet so rarely do we glimpse real faces that “illuminate the complexities of race, freedom, and agency before, during, and after the Civil War,” says the National Gallery of Art, which presents Remember Me: Picturing African Americans in Early Photography later this year. The exhibition brings forward dozens of images taken of and by Black Americans, showcasing a wide variety of lived experiences in one place.

Fashion, family, and social status are on full display in a range of gelatin silver prints, daguerrotypes, tintypes, and ambrotypes, some of which are colorized. Because many of the earliest formats were very fragile, they were often displayed in ornate folding cases. Several of these will be included with their images, plus cabinet cards and portraits by pioneering Black artists like James Van Der Zee, who ran a prominent studio in Harlem in the early 20th century.

The exhibition will highlight around 70 pieces in the museum’s collection that center self-expression and the entrepreneurial spirit of African American individuals. Remember Me is slated to open on November 7 and will continue through March 14 in Washington, D.C. Learn more and plan your visit on the museum’s website.

items.title: A Keyring Camera That’s Not Digital. Try the Baby Holga! by Alec Pain
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Alec Pain (Alastair Place)

I recently purchased a digital keychain/keyring made by Holga (find on eBay). It’s similar to the Kodak Charmera, only it’s been beautifully designed to replicate their old “Baby” Holga, the Holga Micro 110.

It got me thinking about how nice it would be to re-make it – and provide analog film photographers with a keychain/keyring that isn’t digital! I’ve asked Holga and … there’s a possibility… but I think I’ll need a large number of you to buy one!

Find the Holga Digital Keychain on eBay here and the Baby Holga/Holga Micro 110 on eBay here.

110 Film Photography

There are two fantastic articles written by my fellow Shoot it with film writers about 110 film photography. The first is by Angela Izzo: 110 Film: What Is It & Everything You Need to Know.

The second is by Katya Rowny: Pentax Auto 110 Review: A Nostalgic and Unique Pocket Film Camera.

Where to Buy a Baby Holga

If you do a search for the Baby Holga or Holga Micro 110 on eBay, you’ll find that it came in a number of different colors. I have the Yellow, Red, and actually Black. The latter formed part of an Oyakö set of a Baby Holga and a Mummy/Daddy Holga 120FN and distributed by superheadz.

The others are very tricky to get hold of, with Red the most available. Ebay has a couple – and the cost has started to rise for such a little camera!

My advice? The Japanese website buyee.jp – an excellent website for locating old and out of production Holgas, Dianas, and plastic cameras! They “buy” the camera for you and take care of the postage for a small fee and you can also buy several things and have everything posted at once.

How to Use the Baby Holga

In the meantime, I’ve started taking pictures with the Holga Micro again. Essentially, it’s a very, very simple camera. It means you need to think carefully about what you are going to take and be mindful of the camera’s lack of control.

The camera (according to instructions if you are lucky enough to find one with the camera when buying secondhand) has a focal length of 25mm, an F8 aperture and a shutter speed of 1/125 second. The focus is 1m to infinity. Pretty much standard Holga in terms of the aperture and shutter speed.

To load the camera, you pull down the back cover (it can be a little tight) and pop your 110 film cartridge in. Close the back cover, and then wind the film advance wheel (located at the front of the camera on the right when the “lens” is facing you) until it reaches the first number. It should stop there. If it doesn’t, take the cartridge back out and make sure it is inserted properly.

The Viewfinder is folded neatly on the top of your camera so needs to be pulled up with your thumb or finger, in order to compose your shot. Hold the camera around 4-5 cms away from your eye when looking through it, and depress the tiny shutter release button on the back (right) of the camera. Then, wind onto the next shot.

Bear in mind that the camera is either on the end of your keyring or in your pocket, so if you are going to put it away, the button can often be pressed accidentally. If you have finished shooting for the time being, it’s best to not forward the film to the next number as you might end up with the odd blank shot.

Film Available for 110 Cameras

Lomography is the only company right now producing 110 film. There are various expired films available, but for the purposes of this article I’ve not shot Orca (I have a roll being developed!) or Classicolour. I couldn’t tell the difference with the Color ‘92s when I came to scanning them:

Lomography B&W Orca 110 ISO 100
Lomography LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200
Lomography Lobster Redscale 110 ISO 200
Lomography Color Tiger 110 ISO 200
Lomography LomoChrome Turquoise 110 ISO 100–400
Lomography LomoChrome 2021 Metropolis 110 ISO 100–400
Lomography LomoChrome Color ’92 ISO 400
Lomography LomoChrome Color 92 Sun Kissed ISO 400
Lomography LomoChrome Purple 110 ISO 400

There are a couple of triple packs available, too, but the savings are minimal.

Taking the Baby Holga Out

Previously, I had shot it during Holga Week on a trip to Norwich and Cromer. I was most impressed with the portraits I took of my friend the photographer @jayhaldon:

You can see some light leaking onto the bottom of the film but not the actual image. This being a Holga, you’ll find that the light leaks can sometimes edge onto the image area. I think shooting into the sun doesn’t help.

I love the way that the image ghosts itself in various degrees onto the surroundings, and I think I prefer seeing the Lomochrome writing on top of the image.

More casual “street” shots at Norwich station also came out well and benefitted from the 400 ISO film.

More recently, I’ve been testing several of the cameras I have. Here’s a shot pointing into the sun (barely shielded by a light cloud), but it still produces a pleasing image, and I was able to find some detail in the shadows with LomoChrome Tiger ISO200.

Related: The Holga 135 Pan: Getting to Know Your Camera

LomoChrome Turquoise

LomoChrome Turquoise seemed to produce the best images – perhaps because I was pointing the camera at London landmarks.

As you can see from the image on the second image below, it does take some getting used to when looking through the viewfinder with the Palace of Westminster trying to get in on the scene!

I took some portraits of my wife with the camera, and you can see the sun behind her creeping into the picture:

And flowers always look good on Turquoise:

Scanning (and Developing) Your Tiny Negatives

I did find scanning the negatives problematic. The images are tiny and my scanner (an Epson V700 photo) went from producing beautiful images like those below to very grainy pictures which I couldn’t improve.

There is a 110 film holder available here, but you could also use Lomography’s digitaliza. I’m waiting for mine, but I scanned the negatives on my flatbed scanner – with two pieces of glass holding them. I managed to get a reasonable resolution on them, but not always!

You can also develop the negatives yourself. I bought two little reels from @Film Stuff Lab in the US which was very reasonable if you live in the States, and I hope to start developing soon! I also found these 110 reels on Amazon.

The smaller your negative, the larger your hairs and icks, so get used to using the healing tool in Photoshop!

Looking at the two here side-by-side of Big Ben, I’m still not sure which I prefer.

LomoChrome Metropolis

LomoChrome Metropolis also seemed suited to the brighter sunshine. The Lomo 92 seemed to struggle in really bright light (unlike the Mummy/Daddy Holgas).

LomoChrome Tiger

Tiger was also lovely in bright sunlight – note the light leaks:

And here’s a missing frame when placing the Holga in my pocket, traveling from (19) Oxford Street window to next day (21) the South Bank:

You can also get some inconsistencies when scanning:

And I did seem to get a few scratches on my Yellow Holga – along with some moiré when scanning too:

Lomo 92

A trip to Scotland gave me the chance to try out some landscapes, and these, too, were a little inconsistent when scanning:

In cloudy conditions in Weston-Super-Mare, Lomo 92 produced muddy and duller imagery.

Lomo Redscale “Lobster”

I did love this Redscale study of a High Rise in Lewisham:

The Baby Holga Project

It’s safe to say that I have renewed my love for the Baby Holga, so much so that I have started a little project: The Baby Holga Project (@thebabyholga). I already owned two of the Baby Holgas, an orange and a black one, and have since purchased quite a few more.

I have started sending them around the world. Currently, there are four travelling around the US. Three are in the UK, three in Europe, one in Hong Kong, one in Argentina, one in Canada, one in Africa and two in Australia/New Zealand.

Check out the Instagram page to see what’s happening or who has which Holga. If you would like to participate, please DM @thedailyholga or @thebabyholga.

Thank you so much, Alec! Alec is a regular contributor here at Shoot It With Film, and be sure to check out his other articles, like No Tripod? No Problem. Double Exposures with Neon, LED Screens, & Contact Sheets and The Holga Challenge: 18 Photography Prompts with the Holga & Kentmere Film.

You can also check out more of his work on Instagram.

Leave your questions about the Baby Holga below in the comments, and pick one up for yourself on eBay! You can also pick up the digital Holga keychain on eBay here.

items.title: Alice Jankovic
items.excerpt: PHROOM
items.content:
PHROOM

ALICE JANKOVIC

Green Paradox

Instagram
website

 

The Green Paradox project was born during the Swit artist residency in Gothenburg in September 2025 and developed around the figure of Scheele Green, an 18th-century pigment of extraordinary brilliance but intrinsically toxic. Discovered by chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele, who studied and worked at the ancient pharmacy Apoteket Enhörningen (the “Unicorn Pharmacy”), this color becomes the fulcrum of a visual investigation that explores the paradox between aesthetic beauty and invisible danger.

The work is configured as a chromatic archaeology in which archival images and contemporary photographs intertwine to trace a subtle line between the history of science, myth, and the transformation of matter.

The essential counterpart of this research is the city of Gothenburg, voted “Europe’s greenest city”: an urban lung where nature expresses a living and regenerating breath, placing itself in dialectical antithesis to the mineral toxicity of the historic pigment. Through an act of photographic listening, the work deconstructs the legacy of a color that still questions our present. The result is a complex chorus where chemistry meets ecology and memory becomes image, transforming the history of a color into a poetic reflection on the fragility of the balance between humanity and the environment. Scheele’s Green thus becomes the lens through which to observe nature’s capacity to persist and change, between aesthetic appeal and contemporary awareness.

Born in Genoa, Alice Jankovic is a visual artist and photographer with a solid interdisciplinary background. After completing art school, her passion for photography was ignited during a year spent in Sweden, where her encounter with Nordic light became a profound inspiration for her visual research.
After returning to Italy, she broadened her academic perspective by attending the Academy of Fine Arts in Venice (New Technologies for the Visual Arts) and, subsequently, the Academy of Genoa (Art Education). Desiring, however, to fully immerse herself in photography and specialize in a targeted manner, she interrupted her academic studies to move to Milan, where she completed a two-year intensive program at the Italian Institute of Photography (IIF). Her growing passion for publishing and photo editing led her to further explore the connection between image, text, and storytelling, attending the Photography and Literature course at the Jack London school in the Marche region and several specialized workshops in visual storytelling.
Her research focuses on the intersection of photography, installation, and editorial, evolving into a form of “visual archaeology” that integrates digital and analog photography and archival materials.
Influenced by myth and literature, the artist deconstructs the image to recontextualize it, transforming the photographic act into a tool for investigating memory. Through a constant dialogue between past and present, her works interrogate the human imprint on the landscape, hovering between documentation and evocation.

items.title: Im Halbschatten: Echoes of a Forgotten Dress
items.content: By engaging with the history of the Jewish fashion industry in Germany and its systematic, forced Aryanization during National Socialism, the project examines what remains hidden or forgotten, yet continues to be passed down subconsciously through generations. The original dress carries the physical traces of these political transformations, visible in its pattern, fabric, and construction. Through careful analysis and deconstruction, new garments emerged from this history. Moritz and Daria—who is Jewish herself—become the physical vessels through which the complex gender dynamics between Walther and Gertraud are reconsidered. Materially, thick wool layers conceal delicate silk underneath; one has to literally move through these heavy layers to uncover the shadows passed down through generations, lingering beneath the skin. Through motion, unexpected openings reveal the hidden, delicate fabrics and intricate embroidery beneath. Daria’s trousers, worn in the photographs by Ludwig, open through embroidered pockets that directly reference the domestic textile work idealized onto women, contrasting sharply with rigid military pattern construction. All three trousers in the collection feature an extra-deep crotch, prioritizing comfort, free movement, and an exploration of androgyny. Constructed from a mixture of deadstock fabrics, leftovers, and antique flea market finds, the collection balances historical gravity with contemporary utility. Despite their historical weight, these clothes are meant to be lived in—to move, to play, and possibly even to play football in. Captured on a Sunday afternoon at Humboldthain in Berlin by photographer Ida Weber, the accompanying imagery utilizes two analogue formats to catch the models in fluid motion, blending the ghosts of the past with the vitality of the present.

items.title: Defiance and pride in Chicano Camera Culture
items.excerpt: A Photographic History — A new major exhibition surveys Mexican American photography over six decades, platforming Chicano artists at a Chicano museum for the first time. Skyrocketing to fame in the late 1970s, comedia
items.content:
A Photographic History — A new major exhibition surveys Mexican American photography over six decades, platforming Chicano artists at a Chicano museum for the first time.

Skyrocketing to fame in the late 1970s, comedian Cheech Marin parlayed his position as one half of beloved stoner duo Cheech & Chong to become one of the world’s leading proponents of Chicano (Mexican American) art. In 2022, the Cheech Marin Center for Chicano Art & Culture, aka The Cheech, opened its doors, making history as the first museum devoted exclusively to “all things Chicano art”.

Hailing from Los Angeles, curator Elizabeth Ferrer remembers the museum’s opening as an important event, both for the community and for herself. Recognising she was among like minds, she set forth to create Chicano Camera Culture: A Photographic History, 1966-2026, an epic celebration of Chicano life as seen through 150 works across multiple generations now on view at the Cheech.

Featuring nearly 50 photographers including trailblazers Louis Carlos Bernal, George Rodriguez, and María Varela; innovators Reynaldo Rivera, Kathy Vargas, and Ken Gonzales-Day; and contemporary artists Guadalupe Rosales, Star Montana, and Thalía Gochez, Chicano Camera Culture forms a map of photographic history that has been largely disregarded by industry and institutions alike. 

  • Read next: Down and out in east LA: vintage shots of Chicano life

“The photographic record, whether from the viewpoint of photojournalists, documentarians, hobbyists, or artists, was created by the white gaze, and for a long time that fact was by and large taken for granted,” Ferrer says. “With the rise of the Civil Rights movement, the Chicano gaze comes into play. This means that for the first time, Chicanos are representing other Chicanos, typically, people who would otherwise be anonymous or unrecognised.” 

Like Ferrer’s 2021 book, Latinx Photography in the United States: A Visual History, Chicano Camera Culture is a landmark work, exploring Chicano photography as a cultural ethos born from knowledge of self. Rather than ascribe descriptors to identity, Ferrer maps its expression across generations, exploring the age-old questions of the human condition with a tender heart and a knowing eye. 

“All of the work in the show illuminates in one way or another, what it means to be Chicano,” she says. “Many of the themes addressed by the photographers – pride in identity, our struggle for agency and autonomy, the values we place in family and home, and the ways we create and claim space – are unsurprising. But what is impressive is the innovative ways in which they have been elaborated.” 

  • Read next: Vibrant photos of L.A.’s contemporary lowrider culture

Organised around themes of self/portraiture, domestic life, protests, border stories, and alternate realities, Chicano Camera Culture is a magnificent archive of collective resistance against an occupying force that has vilified and criminalised indigenous and mestizo communities, while telling the stories of the people and their cultures.

“From the beginning, the Chicano gaze has been about expressing pride in Chicano identity, preserving our history, uplifting cultural and spiritual values, validating persons out of the mainstream, and giving visibility to members of our own community,” Ferrer says. “As for what it means to tell Chicano stories by Chicano artists in a Chicano museum in the United States in 2026, I’d say it’s high time!” 

Chicano Camera Culture: A Photographic History, 1966–2026 is on view through September 6, 2026, at the Cheech Marin Art Center in Riverside, California. The catalogue is distributed by the Washington University Press for the Riverside Art Museum.

items.title: ‘Bodega Cats of New York’ Advocates for the City’s Beloved Feline Shopkeepers
items.content:
‘Bodega Cats of New York’ Advocates for the City’s Beloved Feline Shopkeepers

August 5, 2026
BooksPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

In 2022, New York resident and bonafide feline devotee Dan Rimada felt that something needed to be done to shine a light on the city’s cats. The Big Apple not only has a real feral issue, but many of these creatures make their homes in iconic shops found around the city: bodegas. Over time, locals get to know them and they become fixtures of shelves and countertops. Technically, though, New York City considers it a health code violation to have animals in businesses that serve food. In spite of that, thousands of cats serve as mousers and rat catchers, and a lot of people don’t realize that the snoozy tabby nestled atop the Doritos bags is actually illegal.

Rimada founded Bodega Cats of New York to bring visibility to these beloved, informal shop staffers. This fall, a new book published by Epic Ink titled Bodega Cats of New York features 120 photos of 60 cats across all five boroughs along with their stories. The images are snapped by photographer Gulce Kilkis, who also runs the Instagram account @turkish_street_cats.

Advocacy is as much a part of Rimada’s mission as documenting kitties familiar to neighborhood customers, such as Oreo in Park Slope and Prince in SoHo. The type of care or attention the cats get can vary from store to store. Some are treated like royalty, while others are more like interlopers that are tolerated. Nevertheless, Rimada shares their individual stories and raises awareness of the wide range of realities for these animals.

Although they are still in committee, two bills facilitated by Rimada have been introduced that would “stop New York City agencies from treating a cat in a retail food store as an automatic New York City Health Code violation” along with requiring voluntary, free vaccination and spay/neuter programs. The other bill would legally allow cats in retail stores as long as they met veterinary requirements. “We want to protect what makes New York City feel like home,” Rimada says in a statement. “And that includes taking care of the cats that are a part of it.”

Bodega Cats of New York is slated for release in early November. Meet hundreds more feline friends on Instagram, and pre-order your copy on the project’s website. You might also enjoy Marcel Heijnen’s City Cats of Istanbul and a trip through art history with Phaidon’s Cat.

items.content:
Lomography has launched a spectacularly colourful new version of its Lomomatic 110 compact camera for summer.

The new Discomatic version of the 110-format camera is in a colour scheme of dazzling blue, pink and yellow – looking every inch like something that might have been released in the 1980s.

“Summer’s here and we’re ready to relive the heyday of the disco with the popping new Lomomatic 110 Discomatic,” Lomography said in a press release. “This colourful concoction comes with all the exciting features that have made the Lomomatic 110 a favorite among the Lomography Community. A true statement of style and a creative sidekick for life, everyone loves a little funk!

“Don’t be fooled by its size – this creative companion is bursting with big ideas! It’s a thrilling companion for analogue beginners, the sharpest and most trusted 110

camera for seasoned photographers, and a nostalgic voyage for those yearning for the grand old days of 110 film.

“Opening the door to a world of possibilities with a 23mm Minitar Glass Lens, fully automatic settings, controllable ISO, zone focusing, and interchangeable apertures, it can squeeze into all types of small spaces for crazy Lomographic perspectives. Ready for anything, the Lomomatic 110 captures fragments of life; each frame a glimpse into a spontaneous moment frozen in time, effortlessly transformed into a vibrant memory.”

Like other editions of the Lomomatic 110, the camera’s specifications are:

Film format: 110
Lens focal length: 23mm
Available apertures: Day f/5.6, Night f/2.8
Maximum aperture: f/2.8
ISO: controllable 100, 200 or 400
Shutter speed: Auto (A), Bulb (B)
Focusing: Zone focus
Flash: Manual on or off
Multiple exposures: Unlimited
Tripod socket: No
Battery: 1 × CR2 (1.5 V)

The camera is available to order now and costs £109 in the UK along with its matching flash.

items.title: Things Learned and Unlearned: A Conversation with 25KG’s Konstantin Grcic
items.content:
Ontologically, the “thing” is an elusive category—so broad and expansive that it seems to belong more to the realm of ideas than to that of material reality. Yet we live in a culture obsessed with naming, classifying, and pigeonholing every object into a specific function, stabilising its charge and disarming its potential. With 25KG, his latest project, Konstantin Grcic turns the ontological condition of things into the very engine of radicality. Not as an assault on the status quo, as it used to be, but as the introduction of generative doubt: a condition of ambiguity, ambivalence, and multivalence in which objects are meant to be experienced, handled, and lived through unexpected interactions and constantly shifting readings. More than a collection of furniture, 25KG questions the very notion of furnishing itself, opening up new possibilities for how we relate to the things around us. In these pages, Grcic discusses the project and its intersections with both the contemporary design landscape and the traditions that continue to shape it.

Daria Miricola: 25KG is a rather loaded name: it folds together the founding year, 2025, and your initials, but it also reads as a literal unit of weight. Where did the idea originate, and what kind of gravity did you want the label to carry from the outset?

Konstantin Grcic: Ever since I was a child, I knew my initials were the same as ‘kilogram.’ I always liked that—and also the pictogram of the cast-iron weight. So the idea had been with me for a very long time. 25KG was the right moment to use it. Why 25? I needed a name that could be registered as a trademark. And, incidentally, 25 kg is a weight most people can lift—which is why disaster-relief sandbags weigh 25 kg.

DM: The radical design movements of the ‘60s and ’70s operated in open antagonism toward bourgeois domesticity and consumer culture. Do you think the cultural meaning of furniture has shifted since then? In other words: does a radical object still have the same capacity to destabilise the status quo, or has design itself become too self-aware for that?

KG: Yes, I think the meaning of furniture has changed. In the ‘60s and ’70s, radical design still believed objects could directly challenge society. Today, design is much more self-aware—and quickly absorbed by the market, media and culture industry. Even radical gestures become style very fast. But objects can still unsettle us in quieter ways: through ambiguity, discomfort, humour, vulnerability, or by resisting easy categorisation. Perhaps radicality today is less about opposition and more about creating doubt, friction or emotional complexity within everyday life.

DM: More broadly, what is the condition of the European design scene today? Where do you sense genuine vitality, and where do you feel the ﬁeld has become complacent or risk-averse?

KG: There is still a great deal of vitality in the European design scene—especially in smaller, independent structures where design, research, craft and culture overlap more freely. I often find the most interesting work happening at the edges, outside the large commercial system.

At the same time, much of mainstream design has become cautious and overly image-conscious. There is a strong tendency toward safe aesthetics, familiar narratives, and market-friendly ideas. Risk today is often simulated, rather than truly taken.

DM: You have worked for decades within large industrial ecosystems while simultaneously maintaining a highly singular authorial voice. How different is it to operate through your own platform, 25KG, rather than through established clients and manufacturers? What do you gain—and lose—in each model?

KG: Working through my own platform, 25KG, gives me a different kind of freedom and immediacy. Decisions become faster, more instinctive, and sometimes more personal. At the same time, it also means taking responsibility for everything—production, logistics, communication… and risk.

Working with established manufacturers is slower and more complex, but it allows projects to develop with greater industrial depth, technical precision and long-term impact. Ideally, both models nourish each other.

DM: 25KG presents objects simply as ‘THINGS,’ catalogued according to the order in which they appear: THING_01, THING_02, and so on. There is something almost proto-scientiﬁc, or even deadpan, about that protocol.Where does this taxonomy come from?

KG: The taxonomy is intentionally neutral and open. I liked the idea of avoiding predefined categories or narratives and simply letting things appear one after another, almost like findings or observations. The term THING felt direct, unpretentious, and slightly anonymous—which gives the objects more freedom to become whatever people imagine them to be.

DM: The ﬁrst THINGS already seem to share a trajectory or common grammar: raw materials, structural directness, an almost anti-rhetorical clarity. Are you consciously building a language, or do you prefer to let afﬁnities emerge a posteriori?

KG: I’m not trying to build a “language” in a strategic sense. For me, it’s more about attitude. I think there’s a major shortcoming in the industry in this regard. Attitude is something very valuable… but of course it also demands a lot. Strength, confidence, perseverance. The affinities emerge quite naturally through the way we work and what interests us—structure, directness, reduction, certain materials, certain moods. Over time, connections become visible almost by themselves.

DM: How does 25KG approach pricing and communication without falling back on the usual luxury design tropes?

KG: By trying to stay direct and transparent. We avoid artificial narratives of exclusivity and instead focus on the objects themselves—how they are made, used, and communicated. The challenge is to remain accessible without becoming generic, and precise without becoming corporate.

DM: Your work has often generated sharply polarised reactions. Chair_ONE, for instance, is now cult, yet when it ﬁrst appeared it triggered fascination, bewilderment, even ridicule in certain circles. How do you personally relate to the idea of controversy?

I never saw controversy as a goal in itself. Usually, it simply means that something unsettles existing expectations. If a project creates strong reactions, positive or negative, it often means it touched a nerve. Over time, people tend to become more comfortable with things that initially felt strange, and that grows a stronger bond.

DM: And once a controversial object becomes institutionalised—collected by museums, canonised by the market—does it lose part of its original charge? What does it take today for a piece of furniture to still feel genuinely controversial?

KG: Yes, inevitably, once an object becomes familiar, collected, and historically absorbed, part of its disruptive energy disappears. Today, genuinely controversial furniture is probably less about shocking form and more about questioning systems of production, value, use, or desire in subtle and intelligent ways.

DM: Finally, which future THINGS are currently taking shape? And more importantly: are there territories—materially, politically, or culturally—that you still feel design has not fully managed to tap into?

KG: There are several new THINGS taking shape at the moment. What still interests me are territories where design becomes less resolved and more open. I think design still struggles with ambiguity. It often wants to explain too much, optimise too much, behave too correctly.

items.title: Cryptic Photos by Susan kae Grant Plumb the World of Dreams in ‘Night Journey’
items.content:
Cryptic Photos by Susan kae Grant Plumb the World of Dreams in ‘Night Journey’

August 4, 2026
BooksPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

A house spins out of control in a wind storm, animals loom large in the imaginations of children, and mysterious creatures lurk in the darkness of Susan kae Grant’s shadow puppet-like photographs. For more than two decades, the artist has plumbed the mind’s eye, especially what it sees when we sleep. In the early 1990s, she even began collaborating with a researcher in a sleep laboratory at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Study and documentation of what she visualized in her own REM cycle led to phrases and vocabulary about what she dreamt that she continues to tap into for her studio work.

Forthcoming this autumn from MW Editions, Grant’s book Night Journey delves into her lifelong fascination with the realm of the unconscious. Silhouetted figures and objects seemingly float across nearly 100 vignettes that are blurry, cryptic, and stretched around the edges as if they originate from somewhere we’re unable to grasp.

“Through arresting black and white tableaux populated by fantastical creatures, animals, and children in hallucinatory settings, these photographs invite us to traverse the strangeness and chaos of breakneck contemporary life, like the dreams that inspired them,” the publisher says.

See more on the artist’s Instagram, and pre-order Night Journey on the MW Editions’ website.

items.title: Analogue aF-1 release delayed due to ongoing tweaks to prototypes
items.content:
The release of the Analogue aF-1 compact camera – which initially was planned to be produced by the end of last year – has been delayed while its developers fine-tune the pre-production prototypes.

In an email sent out to subscribers, its Amsterdam-based creators said the camera was currently in pre-production, but problems identified in prototypes so far have necessitated delays before the camera can go into full production.

Analogue said it would not “share a delivery date” but would send out more updates as improvements were made.

“When we first announced the aF-1, we genuinely believed we could bring it to market much sooner. Looking back now, that simply wasn’t realistic. If we had known then what we know today, we definitely would have planned some things differently, the team, which is led by Ralph Tilon, said in the update.

“Over the past year and a half, we’ve invested far more time, money, and energy than we ever expected. Not because we have to, but because we genuinely want to build a camera that deserves to exist.

“We’ve learned that building a camera has its own schedule,” the update said. “Rather than continuing to move deadlines, we’d rather keep working, keep sharing meaningful progress, and announce a delivery timeline once we’re confident we can stand behind it.”

The aF-1, announced in January 2025, is a compact 35mm camera with Lidar-based autofocus and a sliding front panel like the Olympus XA or Mju-II. The camera features a 35mm f/2.8 lens and an inbuilt lens. It was a surprise announcement alongside other recent new compact cameras such as the Pentax 17 and the Rollei 35AF.

Designed by the team who also run the camera shop Analogue in Amsterdam, the camera is being manufactured in China. The camera is already available to pre-order for €450 (£390/$512), though the latest update makes it clear that there is, as yet, no confirmed release date.

Earlier this year, Analogue had published another update that said delays in production were caused by modifications to the camera’s auto-focusing unit.

Analogue said: “In about two weeks, we’ll be travelling back to China for another engineering review with our manufacturing partner. We’ll continue sharing updates as we move through the next stage of development and pre-production.”

items.content:
The Top Photos in the CWAS David Malin Awards Highlight Astronomical Wonders

July 31, 2026
Photography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Every year, the Central West Astronomical Society (CWAS) of New South Wales celebrates AstroFest, a festival of astronomy during which amateur photographers and scientists from around the globe are invited to submit their best views of the night sky and beyond. This year, the overall prize was awarded to Stefan Buda for his tonal moonscape titled “The Lunar Apennines,” which captures a detailed view of Montes Apenninus.

Categories include Deep Sky, Solar System, Wide-Field, Nightscapes, and more, allowing photographers to contribute images of phenomena ranging from distant nebulae and spiral galaxies to the Milky Way and aurora australis, or the southern lights, shining above impressive terrestrial landscapes. A 2027 calendar featuring the winning images is available for purchase, and you can see the entire gallery of top shots on the award’s website.

items.title: Point & Shoot Camera Roundup: 3 Film Cameras Worth Checking Out by Katya Rowny
items.content:
This post may contain affiliate links. If you click on a link and make a purchase, Shoot It With Film may receive a small commission at no additional cost to you.

Written by Katya Rowny

Over the past few years, we have had an influx of new film cameras arrive on the scene (talk about an oxymoron!). From the half-frame Pentax 17, to the Rollei 35AF from MiNT, and most recently the Snapic A1 from Kodak.

Unfortunately, most of these cameras are not cheap, with the range being in the $100’s for the Snapic and the $500s for the Pentax 17. I have to admit, I am not impervious to all of these new models and makes, and have been secretly coveting the Snapic A1 for a while.

In an attempt to further dissuade myself from acquiring more cameras, (did you read my other article where I mentioned I have a slight camera hoarding problem?) I decided to re-examine my collection of point and shoots and remember why I fell in love with them in the first place.

1. Chinon Bellami

First up is the Chinon Bellami (find on eBay). Also known as the Revue 35CC in some markets. This camera is one of those surprisingly cool cameras that often flies under the radar. I picked this camera up at a swap meet for under $20 and was drawn in by the size and unique design.

Introduced in 1980 as a competitor to the Olympus XA series, it packs a lot into an incredibly compact body. Instead of a traditional lens cap, the Bellami uses a clever “barn door” mechanism that opens when you advance the film, revealing a sharp 35mm f/2.8 lens Chinonex Color lens.

The Bellami uses automatic exposure, has a fast shutter ranging from 1/8 to 1/1000 second, and simple zone focusing. This camera slips easily into a pocket, has a quiet shutter, and requires very little thought beyond estimating your focus distance. The perfect grab and go camera.

In everyday use, the Bellami proves to be more than just a cute little camera. The camera handles exposure automatically, leaving you free to focus on composing your shot, while simple zone-focus settings keep operation straightforward. I was impressed by the image quality of my prints, noting that the lens produces sharp photos with rich colors and strong contrast despite the camera’s age.

Combined with a satisfying film advance, quiet shutter, and lightweight design, the Bellami is fun and effortless to shoot. While it may not be as well known as some of its contemporaries, It has become one of my main go-to’s when I want to quickly capture memories instead of focus on settings.

Read the full Chinon Bellami review here.

Find the Chinon Bellami on eBay.

2. Olympus XA2

The Olympus XA2 has earned a reputation as one of the best compact film cameras ever made, and it’s easy to see why. I can’t rave about this camera enough; I recommend it to anyone who will listen. Small enough to slip into a pocket, simple enough for beginners, and capable of producing fantastic images, it’s the kind of camera you can take anywhere.

Released in 1980 as a more user-friendly version of the original XA, the XA2 swapped the rangefinder for a simple zone-focus system while keeping the iconic sliding clamshell cover. Paired with the sharp 35mm f/3.5 Zuiko lens and automatic exposure, it offers a great balance between convenience and image quality.

What really makes the XA2 special is how easy it is to shoot and the image quality. Open the lens cover, set the focus zone for your subject, and let the camera do the rest.

This camera is the perfect travel companion and everyday carry camera, thanks to its lightweight design, quiet shutter, and consistently sharp results.

Like any camera that’s over 40 years old, it has a few quirks—aging electronics that may need some extra attention and occasional light leaks can happen—but those drawbacks are minor compared to everything it does well.

I have captured some of my favorite images on this camera, and it has traveled to many countries with me. For anyone looking for a reliable, pocket-sized film camera that delivers great photos without a lot of fuss, the XA2 remains one of the best options out there.

Read the full Olympus XA2 review here.

Find the Olympus XA2 at KEH Camera or on eBay.

Related: 12 Best Point and Shoot Film Cameras

3. Olympus Trip AF

Last but not least, the Olympus Trip AF (find on eBay) is one of those cameras that you may pass over but deserves a second glance, especially if you’re a fan of the legendary Olympus Trip 35.

Introduced in 1984, the Trip AF represented Olympus’s move into the new wave of electronic point-and-shoot cameras. Unlike its metal-bodied predecessor, the Trip AF is mostly plastic and built around convenience. It features a 35mm f/3.5 Zuiko lens, manual film advance and rewind, a built-in flash, and a surprisingly simple autofocus system with just two focus points—roughly 1.5 meters and 4 meters.

Exposure is fully automatic, with shutter speeds ranging from 1/85 to 1/250 second and apertures from f/3.5 to f/11, making it a true grab-and-go camera. You can check out the manual here.

The Trip AF line was part of Olympus’s broader AF (Infinity in the U.S.) family of autofocus compact cameras. Compared with the Trip AF, premium models like the AF-1 offered a faster 35mm f/2.8 lens, closer focusing, a wider range of shutter speeds, DX coding, and accessories like teleconverters and close-up lenses.

The AF-1 Twin expanded the idea with both 35mm and 70mm lenses, while later cameras like the AF-10 XB featured a wide 29mm lens and a large, bright viewfinder. The biggest difference between the Trip and AF models was that Trip cameras focused on maximum simplicity with fixed shutter speeds, while AF models offered more advanced, program-controlled exposure systems.

Find the Olympus Trip AF on eBay.

Final Thoughts

Some of these cameras are more well-known than others, but every one of them has earned its place as a great compact point-and-shoot. Whether you’re just getting started with film or you’ve been shooting for years, you really can’t go wrong with any of them. The right choice simply comes down to how much control you want over your photos.

As tempting as it is to chase the latest hyped-up film camera, I often have to remind myself that I already own some amazing cameras that are more than capable of producing beautiful images. The truth is, there are plenty of affordable and often overlooked cameras out there—you just have to know what features matter most to you and do a little hunting.

The only question that remains is which one will you choose?

Thank you so much, Katya! Katya is a regular contributor for Shoot It With Film, and you can check out her other articles here, such as 12 Months, 12 Cameras: The Film Photography Project That Changed How I Shoot and 5 Unconventional Ways to Find Your Inner Artist.

You can also find more of Katya’s work on her website, Instagram, and YouTube.

Let us know any questions you have about these point and shoot film cameras below in the comments!

items.title: Grainy, yearning memories of Europe’s ’90s free rave heyday
items.excerpt: Never Alone — A new photobook from Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi presents pictures they made over seven years while touring the continent as part of the Tekno Mobil Squad soundsystem crew. It archives parties, people and a li
items.content:
Never Alone — A new photobook from Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi presents pictures they made over seven years while touring the continent as part of the Tekno Mobil Squad soundsystem crew. It archives parties, people and a lifestyle largely consigned to the past.

In 1994, the British government led by John Major passed the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act. It criminalised unlicensed raves, making it illegal for 20 or more people to gather and listen to “sounds wholly or predominantly characterised by the emission of a succession of repetitive beats”.

At the time, UK free party culture had reached its zenith. Crews such as DiY, Spiral Tribe and Circus Warp were organising raves across common land and abandoned buildings around the country, culminating in the 1992 Castlemorton Common rave that attracted tens of thousands of people across the weekend.

Without charging money for entry, and consciously making use of public and dilapidated spaces, free party culture was idealistic and egalitarian. But now faced with the prospect of up to three months in prison for attending or organising raves, some felt that the UK no longer offered the opportunity for them to live the nomadic, free lifestyles that they dreamed of.

  • Read next: Sepia splashed memories of Britain’s ’90s squatting and free party scene

Crews such as Spiral Tribe and Bedlam followed in the footsteps of the Mutoid Waste Company in the late ’80s, setting off across Europe with no end goal, organising parties as they travelled eastwards through France, Germany, the Czech Republic, Italy and beyond. Inspired by the parties and culture, homegrown European crews began popping up and organising their own versions of raves, or “Teknivals” as they were often referred to. 

In 1997, Italian photographers Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi stumbled across their first raves. Both were grew up around Milan and attended the same high school, with Clementi’s parents being involved in the post-hippie and punk movements of the late ’70s and ’80s. Her first rave was on the ex-Breda industrial lands – formerly a huge factory where trains were built. “I first encountered free parties and rave culture around 1997,” Clementi says. “From that moment on, I immediately felt that this was where I belonged.”

Morandi, meanwhile, attended her first in an abandoned factory in Bologna. “I experienced absolute freedom and immediately knew I had found something unique,” she remembers. 

  • Read next: As Italy’s rave culture faces crackdowns, a cyberpunk citadel fights to survive

They both instantly got the bug, as people in the UK had at the beginning of the decade, and similarly-minded rebellious folks across Europe did too. That same year, they founded the Tekno Mobil Squad along with a group of friends, and for the best part of the next decade, Clementi and Morandi travelled Europe, moving beyond Italy’s borders while throwing raves and teknivals in “abandoned factories, former military sites, forests, beaches and open countryside”.

Their new photobook Never Alone: 1997-2004 Raving in Europe, documents the crew’s heyday between 1997 and 2004, filled with nostalgic, black-and-white shots of the time that are part-diaristic and part-documentation of a culture that existed largely hidden away on the fringes of mainstream society. Without their pictures, the time would likely have been consigned to memory.

Clementi and Morandi would take pictures often for no real reason beyond cherishing moments. “We loved photography,” they explain. “At the time, we weren’t consciously documenting history – we were just photographing our lives. Since photography was entirely analogue, very few people were doing it. There was no pressure to document every experience. Every frame mattered. Photographs were memories, not content for social media.”

  • Read next: As Hanoi’s nightlife faces raids & repression, its underground scene modulates

There’s shots of raves in full flow, with huge soundsystems, packed crowds, and DJs spinning techno, acid, jungle, drum & bass and more to dancers, but it’s also the books quieter moments that shine the brightest. Intimate portraits of their friends and pets in their trucks are interspersed with moments relaxing in nature or lying on top of soundsystems. 

The pictures showcase genuine community among the travelling troupe, who moved around Europe in search of nothing but parties, music, creativity and freedom. “We lived on four wheels. The trucks were our homes and carried the soundsystems,” Clementi and Morandi say. “Every weekend we searched for a new location, spreading the word through flyers and word of mouth.” 

Run ins with police were also documented. Different countries and municipalities saw a wide range in responses to their parties. “[We had police encounters] many times,” they explain. “Sometimes they confiscated our trucks or shut down parties. Other times they escorted us to safer locations.”

  • Read next: We took techno legend Chris Liberator to a virtual rave, here’s what went down

As free party culture grew in popularity, and became commercialised into the global festival and nightclub circuit we know today, the images capture the lightning in a bottle moment of the ’90s, in the early, radical days of the movement, before authorities had time to properly organise and legislate to curb it.

The project then, serves as a reminder of a bygone era. “We realised we had a unique archive documenting one of Europe’s most significant underground movements and wanted to turn it into cultural memory,” Morandi and Clementi say. “It is visual memory, freedom, art and hope – a project that tells the story of many lives.”

Never Alone: 1997-2004 Raving in Europe by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi is published by Propaganda / Drago.

items.title: Zac Henderson Venerates Devils Tower in Bold Black-and-White Photos
items.content:
Zac Henderson Venerates Devils Tower in Bold Black-and-White Photos

July 30, 2026
NaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

In 1906, Devils Tower in northeastern Wyoming became the first national monument in the U.S., preserving a little more than 1,300 acres around the 867-foot-tall column of igneous rock. Amid the rolling hills of the plains, it can be seen from miles around, and it’s been a sacred site and gathering place for myriad Indigenous American tribes, who refer to it by names like Bear Lodge or Bear’s House.

One oral narrative describes how bears attacked a group of seven girls, and the ground swelled up to push the children toward the sky. There, they became the constellation Pleiades, or the “Seven Sisters,” which can be seen over the monument. In other stories, the distinctive striations around the landform are said to have been created by bears clawing at the earth to try to reach the girls.

For nomadic photographer Zac Henderson, the unique geological formation proved an irresistible subject. He travels the continent making dreamy images of landscapes and natural phenomena, often merging reality with a sense of the uncanny. When it comes to geology, there’s hardly a more iconic example than Devils Tower, which formed tens of millions of years ago as a column of hardened magma was gradually revealed through erosion.

Henderson captures the moodiness of clouds casting shadows in black-and-white images that are redolent of Ansel Adams’ deep tonal shifts. Even though the monument sees hundreds of thousands of visitors every year, there is a sense of isolation and unadulterated wonder, as if we are encountering it for the first time. Henderson also captures the changing light and otherworldly textures and ochres of the rock face, which can be seen from a network of paths around its one-mile base circumference.

See more timelapses on Henderson’s Vimeo, and explore more on Behance.

items.title: Kolios: emptiness and Negative Space
items.content:
KOILOS—derived from the ancient Greek word κοῖλος, meaning hollow, concave, or cavity—serves as the foundational concept for a fashion story photographed by Marcello Ferri and styled and art-directed by Mariia Khrebtova. Rooted in a minimal visual language, the project pivots away from loud, performative expressions of femininity, choosing instead to explore softness, silence, and sculptural form as a nuanced visual and emotional language.

The narrative treats the female form not as a mere figure, but as an architectural presence that interacts intimately with light, fabric, and surrounding space. Emptiness and negative space are given primary agency; the body functions almost like a sculpted object inhabiting an environment, creating a subtle yet palpable tension between presence and absence, fragility and structure.

Drawing heavily from an architectural sensibility, the story operates on the principle that void and silence themselves have the power to define atmosphere, shape raw emotion, and mold physical form into an introspective celebration of quiet femininity.
